## 8. TERMS OF SERVICE — enforceability is a UI problem, not a drafting problem.

**The test (9th Cir., *Berman v. Freedom Financial Network*, 33 F.4th 1123 (2022)):** absent actual knowledge, an online contract binds only if **(1)** the site provides **reasonably conspicuous notice** of the terms, **and (2)** the user takes an action that **unambiguously manifests assent**. https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2022/04/05/20-16900.pdf

**Berman failed even though the page said "I understand and agree to the Terms & Conditions."** A large green "Continue" button did not convey the **legal significance** of the click. That is the bar. Browsewrap (a footer link, no action) is **routinely unenforceable**. Clickwrap (affirmative check + "I agree") is **routinely enforced**.

**What the site must do at signup:**
- An **unchecked checkbox** the user affirmatively ticks. Never pre-checked. Never inferred from a "Sign up" click alone.
- Notice text **immediately adjacent** to the action button, **in the same visual field**, no scrolling required, **contrasting**, **≥ the size** of surrounding body text — not grey 10px under the fold.
- **Hyperlinks visually distinguishable** — contrasting color (blue) **and** underlined — resolving to the actual ToS and Privacy Policy.
- Button copy that makes the **legal significance explicit**: "**By creating an account, I agree to the Terms of Service and Privacy Policy**" + "Create account."
- **Evidence, or it didn't happen**: log and immutably retain `user_id`, `timestamp`, `IP`, `user_agent`, **the exact version identifier/hash of the ToS as rendered**, and a snapshot of the signup screen. Courts demand proof of **what the user saw**. Screenshot the flow at each release.
- **Version the ToS.** On **material** change, **re-present and re-collect assent** — "continued use constitutes acceptance" clauses are weak-to-worthless for material changes, and a unilateral-amendment clause without notice can render the **whole agreement illusory** (*Douglas v. U.S. Dist. Court*, 9th Cir.).
- **Language**: the UI is French and the users are Moroccan. **Present the assent text in the language of the UI.** A French-speaking user clicking through English-only terms is an assent argument you lose.

**Clauses to include:** arbitration + class waiver (needs **heightened** conspicuousness; weigh CA **mass-arbitration** fee exposure — it can cost more than the claims), governing law + venue (Wyoming; but note **consumer-protection statutes and TCPA rights are generally not waivable by contract**, and a foreign-user forum clause may be unenforceable abroad), limitation of liability, warranty disclaimers, **the seller-consent/indemnity stack from §4**, acceptable use, suspension/termination, **the OFAC representations from §10**, DMCA agent if there is UGC, and a **DPA/processor addendum** (incorporated by reference) covering the end-customer data.

## 9. ACCESSIBILITY — no rule, real risk, and the mitigation product is itself an FTC defendant.

- **There is NO DOJ regulation setting a technical standard for private-business (Title III) websites.** DOJ's position: "the Department does not have a regulation setting out detailed standards," but the ADA's general nondiscrimination and effective-communication provisions **do apply to the web**, and existing technical standards "provide helpful guidance." https://www.ada.gov/resources/web-guidance/
- **The 2024 web rule is Title II ONLY** — state/local government, 28 CFR Part 35 Subpart H, **WCAG 2.1 Level AA**. **It does not reach private businesses.** DOJ's **April 2026 interim final rule extended** those deadlines: entities ≥50,000 population → **26 Apr 2027**; <50,000 and special districts → **26 Apr 2028**. **Irrelevant to iGrowFast except as the government's chosen benchmark.**
- **Practical standard: WCAG 2.1 AA.** It is what the Title II rule adopted, what DOJ's Title III settlements and consent decrees have used for a decade, and what courts reach for. (W3C's current rec is WCAG 2.2 AA; building to 2.2 AA costs little more and is strictly safer.)
- **Litigation risk** is private, not regulatory. **Circuit split** on whether a website with no physical nexus is a "place of public accommodation": 1st and 7th Circuits lean yes; **3rd, 6th, 9th, 11th require a nexus to a physical place**. **Wyoming sits in the 10th** — but **plaintiffs choose the forum**, and they file in **SDNY/EDNY, S.D. Fla., and C.D. Cal.** The real driver is **state law**: California's **Unruh Civil Rights Act** provides a **$4,000 statutory minimum per violation** plus fees (no actual damages needed), and NY State/City Human Rights Law analogues. Thousands of suits and demand letters annually; typical settlements **$5k–$25k** plus remediation.
- **Risk profile for this company today: LOW-MODERATE.** B2B SaaS, no physical location, no US customers, 10th Circuit domicile. It rises the moment there is a US-facing marketing site with a public signup — which is exactly what is being built.
- **Ship on the public site**: keyboard navigation with visible focus, 4.5:1 text contrast, alt text, programmatic form labels, semantic headings/landmarks, no autoplay, respects `prefers-reduced-motion`, accessible names on icon buttons, and an **accessibility statement** naming WCAG 2.1 AA as the target plus a contact for accommodation requests.
- **⚠️ DO NOT buy an accessibility overlay as the fix.** The FTC ordered **accessiBe to pay $1,000,000** (complaint Jan 2025, final order Apr 2025) for **falsely claiming its AI widget could make any website WCAG-compliant** — and, separately, for **formatting paid third-party articles and reviews to look like independent opinions** while hiding the material connection. Overlays do not cure the underlying defects, courts have not accepted them as a defense, and repeating a vendor's compliance claim on your own site is **your** §5 problem. https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2025/01/ftc-order-requires-online-marketer-pay-1-million-deceptive-claims-its-ai-product-could-make-websites

## 10. EXPORT CONTROLS / OFAC — the "worldwide COD" pitch is the exposure. Get the country list right.

**Why it binds:** iGrowFast LLC is a **US person**. OFAC prohibitions attach to US persons **wherever located** and to their foreign branches, and **liability is STRICT** — no intent required. "We didn't know the user was in Iran" is not a defense.

**⚠️ GET THE LIST RIGHT — the standard boilerplate is now WRONG.** Comprehensive/territorial programs as of July 2026:
- **Cuba, Iran, North Korea** — comprehensive.
- **Crimea, and the so-called DNR/LNR regions of Ukraine** (post-2022 measures also cover Kherson/Zaporizhzhia) — territorial.
- **SYRIA IS NO LONGER SANCTIONED.** **E.O. 14312 ("Providing for the Revocation of Syria Sanctions," 30 June 2025, effective 1 July 2025)** terminated the national emergency and revoked E.O.s 13338, 13399, 13460, 13572, 13573, 13582. **The Syrian Sanctions Regulations, 31 CFR Part 542, were REMOVED from the CFR on 26 August 2025.** https://ofac.treasury.gov/recent-actions/20250825 · https://ofac.treasury.gov/recent-actions/20250630 — **Listing Syria as an embargoed jurisdiction in the Terms would be a stale and inaccurate term.** Every ToS template on the internet still lists it. Specific persons (Assad et al.) remain SDNs under **other** authorities (e.g. E.O. 13894 as amended) — which is exactly why the Terms should reference **the SDN List**, not a hand-maintained country list.
- **Russia, Belarus, Venezuela** — targeted/sectoral, **not** territorial embargoes. Do not describe them as embargoed.
- **Morocco is not sanctioned.** The current business is clean. The **"worldwide" positioning** is what creates the surface.

**Screening obligation:** screen at signup and **periodically re-screen** against the **SDN List** and the **Consolidated Sanctions List**, plus the **50 Percent Rule** (an entity ≥50% owned, directly or indirectly, in the aggregate, by one or more blocked persons is **itself blocked** even if unlisted). Geo-IP alone is insufficient but is the minimum. **Log the screening** — the record is what mitigates the penalty. https://ofac.treasury.gov/sanctions-programs-and-country-information

**What the Terms MUST say (verbatim-grade):**
1. **User representation and warranty**: you are not **located in**, **ordinarily resident in**, or **organized under the laws of** any comprehensively sanctioned jurisdiction; you are **not an SDN or otherwise blocked person**, and are not **owned 50% or more or controlled** by one; you are not on **BIS's Entity List / Denied Persons List**.
2. **Use restriction**: you will not use, access, or make the Service available **on behalf of** any such person or from any such jurisdiction, and will not **export or re-export** the Service or its output to them.
3. **Right to suspend, terminate, refuse service, and BLOCK funds** without notice and **without refund** where blocking is required by law. (A refund of blocked property is itself a prohibited transaction — this clause must survive the refund policy in §7.)
4. **Compliance flow-down**: user complies with all applicable export-control and sanctions laws, including the **EAR (15 CFR Parts 730–774)** and OFAC regulations, and with anti-corruption laws (**FCPA**) — relevant to COD cash handling across borders.
5. **Survival + no-waiver**: these obligations survive termination and cannot be waived.

**EAR note:** hosted SaaS is generally **not** an "export" of software (no code is transferred), but **access provisioning to a restricted party can be**, and any **downloadable client, SDK, or mobile app with encryption** may need an **ECCN 5D992.c self-classification report** or qualify for **License Exception ENC / mass-market treatment**. Low priority today; becomes real with a distributed app.

**Penalties:** IEEPA civil penalties are the greater of a statutorily-capped amount per violation (**~$377,700**, inflation-adjusted — *verify the current figure at ofac.treasury.gov*) **or twice the transaction value**; criminal up to **$1,000,000** and **20 years**. Strict liability on the civil side.

## CROSS-CUTTING: WHAT THE THREE HARD CONSTRAINTS COST

| Constraint | Verdict | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| **Founder names never appear** | ✅ **Fully safe.** | No US law requires naming natural persons on a website or in a policy. WY doesn't publish members/managers. CAN-SPAM needs an **address**, not a name. ROSCA/ARL need the **billing entity name** (`iGrowFast LLC`), not a human. **Caveat:** if an executive personally directs a violation, personal liability attaches regardless of website anonymity — see the two Amazon executives charged individually in the $2.5B ROSCA order. Anonymity on the site ≠ anonymity in an enforcement action. |
| **EIN never published** | ✅ **Fully safe.** | No US law requires it. Publishing it is a pure downside (identity-theft/fraudulent-filing vector). W-9s go to counterparties privately. |
| **Processor disclosed only as a generic category** | ✅ **Sufficient — with three conditions.** | No US regime requires naming a vendor; all require **categories** (Oregon's specific-third-parties right is the lone exception and doesn't apply). **Conditions:** (1) the policy must **not** say or imply US-only storage — it must **affirmatively disclose international transfer and EU/German processing**; (2) it must disclose that **WhatsApp message content** is transmitted through and processed by that category; (3) it must not contain any "we don't share with third parties" language. Break any of these and the omission converts from lawful reticence into a §5 half-truth — the *Nomi*/*Avast* pattern. **Separately: US website law does not require naming, but the seller-client DPAs almost certainly will require subprocessor disclosure and a notice/objection right. That is a contract obligation, not a website one, and it is where this constraint will actually bite.** |

## THE HOLE IN THIS SCOPE

The analysis was scoped to US law and delivers a clean answer: the US surface is thin and the constraints are satisfiable. **But the actual data-protection risk for this company is not American.** Data subjects are Moroccan (**Law 09-08**, CNDP — which requires **notification/authorization filings** for processing and for cross-border transfers), infrastructure is German (**GDPR Art. 3(1) establishment-by-servers is arguable; Art. 28 processor duties, Art. 44–49 transfers, and Art. 30 records are live**), and **WhatsApp message content** is Art. 9-adjacent special-category-risk material. **A US-law-only compliance posture on a Morocco/Germany data estate is the real exposure, and no page on the website fixes it.** Commission that analysis separately before the privacy policy is finalized — the policy text is downstream of it.

The FTC submitted a draft ANPRM to OIRA on January 30, 2026; a successor rule is pending. Build to the vacated rule's standard now — ROSCA and state ARLs already compel nearly all of it, and re-engineering a checkout twice costs more.
requirements.where_it_lands: Non-website: product roadmap decision

requirements.requirement: ROSCA enforcement is live and expensive despite the vacatur: Amazon $2.5B (Sept 25, 2025 — $1B civil penalty + $1.5B redress, ~35M consumers, and TWO NAMED EXECUTIVES personally charged); Chegg $7.5M (Sept 15, 2025 — charged ~200k consumers after cancellation requests); FTC v. Uber pending (April 2025). A ROSCA violation is treated as an FTC rule violation, carrying CMPs of $53,088 per violation plus redress. Note personal liability survives website anonymity.
requirements.where_it_lands: Non-website: risk register / board briefing

requirements.requirement: Refund policy must be truthful, pre-purchase, and CONSISTENT across every surface (landing page, ads, in-app copy, support macros). 'No refunds' is lawful if clearly disclosed before purchase, but may not defeat the ROSCA/ARL right to stop future charges, and any contradiction anywhere is a Section 5 deception. Note the California ARL remedy: non-compliant goods/services are deemed an UNCONDITIONAL GIFT — i.e., full refund of everything ever charged.
requirements.where_it_lands: Refund Policy page + all marketing surfaces

requirements.requirement: Signup must use clickwrap: an UNCHECKED checkbox the user affirmatively ticks; notice text immediately adjacent to the action button in the same visual field with no scrolling; contrasting color and at least the size of surrounding body text; hyperlinks visually distinguishable (contrasting color AND underlined) resolving to the actual ToS and Privacy Policy; button copy making the legal significance explicit. Per Berman v. Freedom Financial Network, 33 F.4th 1123 (9th Cir. 2022), a 'Continue' button next to 'I understand and agree to the Terms' FAILED the test. Browsewrap (footer link only) is unenforceable.
requirements.where_it_lands: Signup page

requirements.requirement: Log and immutably retain assent evidence: user_id, timestamp, IP, user_agent, and the exact version identifier/hash of the ToS AS RENDERED, plus a snapshot of the signup screen per release. Courts require proof of what the user actually saw, not what the current ToS says.
requirements.where_it_lands: Non-website: signup backend + evidence retention

requirements.requirement: Present the assent text in the language of the UI. The product UI is French and users are Moroccan — a French-speaking user clicking through English-only terms is an assent argument you lose. Version the ToS and RE-PRESENT for fresh assent on material change; 'continued use constitutes acceptance' is weak for material changes, and a unilateral-amendment clause without notice can render the whole agreement illusory.
requirements.where_it_lands: Signup page + ToS versioning system

requirements.requirement: Terms must contain OFAC representations: user is not located in, ordinarily resident in, or organized under the laws of a comprehensively sanctioned jurisdiction; is not an SDN or blocked person nor owned 50%-or-more/controlled by one (the 50 Percent Rule); is not on BIS's Entity List or Denied Persons List; will not use or make the Service available on behalf of such persons or export/re-export to them; iGrowFast may suspend, terminate, refuse service and BLOCK FUNDS without notice and without refund where required by law (this clause must survive the refund policy); user complies with the EAR (15 CFR 730-774), OFAC regulations, and the FCPA. Obligations survive termination.
requirements.where_it_lands: Terms of Service page — export controls / sanctions section

requirements.requirement: DO NOT list Syria as an embargoed jurisdiction — every ToS template still does and it is now WRONG. E.O. 14312 (June 30, 2025, effective July 1, 2025) revoked the Syria sanctions program and the Syrian Sanctions Regulations (31 CFR Part 542) were REMOVED from the CFR on August 26, 2025. Current comprehensive/territorial programs: Cuba, Iran, North Korea, and the Crimea/DNR/LNR (and Kherson/Zaporizhzhia) regions of Ukraine. Russia, Belarus and Venezuela are targeted/sectoral, NOT territorial embargoes — do not describe them as embargoed. Reference the SDN List rather than a hand-maintained country list, which goes stale.
requirements.where_it_lands: Terms of Service page — sanctions section

requirements.requirement: Implement OFAC screening at signup and periodic re-screening against the SDN List and the Consolidated Sanctions List, applying the 50 Percent Rule. Liability is STRICT — 'we didn't know the user was in Iran' is not a defense. Geo-IP alone is insufficient but is the minimum. LOG every screening; the record is what mitigates the penalty. IEEPA civil penalties: greater of ~$377,700 per violation (inflation-adjusted — verify current figure) or twice the transaction value; criminal up to $1M and 20 years.
requirements.where_it_lands: Non-website: signup/KYC pipeline + audit log

requirements.requirement: Any testimonial, review, case study, or results claim on the marketing site must comply with the Consumer Reviews and Testimonials Rule, 16 CFR Part 465 (in effect since October 21, 2024): no fake or AI-generated reviews, no insider/employee/relative testimonials without a clear material-connection disclosure, no buying or disseminating reviews known or reasonably knowable to be false. CMPs up to $53,088 per violation; the FTC sent warning letters in December 2025. Results claims ('sellers grew 3x') additionally need substantiation and typicality disclosure under the Endorsement Guides, 16 CFR Part 255.
requirements.where_it_lands: Landing page / testimonials / case-study sections

requirements.requirement: Do not describe 30 N Gould St Ste R as 'our headquarters' or 'our office', and do not claim a 'US-based team' or 'US-based support' unless they exist. Using the address as the required legal-notice/CAN-SPAM address is correct and fine; representing a mass-registration virtual address as a real operating office while operations are Morocco-centric is a Section 5 deception that is trivially provable by a competitor or a journalist.
requirements.where_it_lands: Contact page / About page / footer / all marketing copy

requirements.requirement: Build the public site to WCAG 2.1 AA (2.2 AA preferred — marginal extra cost, strictly safer): keyboard navigation with visible focus, 4.5:1 text contrast, alt text, programmatic form labels, semantic headings/landmarks, accessible names on icon buttons, no autoplay, respects prefers-reduced-motion. Publish an accessibility statement naming WCAG 2.1 AA as the target plus a contact for accommodation requests. There is NO DOJ regulation for Title III private-business websites — the 2024 WCAG 2.1 AA rule is Title II (state/local government) ONLY, and DOJ's April 2026 interim final rule extended those deadlines to April 26, 2027 / April 26, 2028. Risk is private litigation, driven by California's Unruh Act ($4,000 statutory minimum per violation plus fees) and NY HRL analogues, not by a federal rule.
requirements.where_it_lands: Public marketing site + Accessibility Statement page

requirements.requirement: DO NOT buy an accessibility overlay as the compliance fix, and never repeat a vendor's compliance claim on your own site. The FTC ordered accessiBe to pay $1,000,000 (complaint January 2025, final order April 2025) for falsely claiming its AI widget could make any website WCAG-compliant — and separately for formatting paid third-party articles to look like independent reviews while hiding the material connection. Overlays do not cure underlying defects and courts have not accepted them as a defense.
requirements.where_it_lands: Non-website: vendor selection decision

requirements.requirement: Wyoming imposes NO website or disclosure requirements: no comprehensive privacy law (2022 HB0086, 2024 HB0163 and 2025 SF0065 all failed to enact), and no law requiring publication of the EIN, members, managers, officers, or any founder name. Wyoming LLCs do not file member/manager identities publicly. The founder-anonymity and EIN-secrecy constraints are fully satisfiable. Wyoming's breach notification law (W.S. 40-12-501 et seq.) and Consumer Protection Act (W.S. 40-12-101 et seq.) exist but the breach law triggers on WY RESIDENTS, not on being a WY LLC — dormant with no WY users.
requirements.where_it_lands: No website page required — confirms the constraint is satisfiable

requirements.requirement: FILING, not a page: Wyoming annual report due the first day of the anniversary month (July 1 each year; first due July 1, 2027), license tax the greater of $60 or $0.0002 per dollar of Wyoming-situs assets. Separately, CONFIRM WITH THE REGISTERED AGENT that the registered-office address of record satisfies the Secretary of State rule — the SoS states that 'post office boxes, drop boxes, virtual addresses, mail forwarding locations, UPS or FedEx stores do not qualify' as a registered office, and 30 N Gould St Ste R is a mass-registration suite. A defective registered office risks administrative dissolution.
requirements.where_it_lands: Non-website: Wyoming SoS filing + registered agent verification

requirements.requirement: VERIFY (medium confidence, not confirmed against an official source in this research): FinCEN's interim final rule of approximately March 26, 2025 exempted US-formed companies from Corporate Transparency Act beneficial-ownership reporting, leaving only foreign reporting companies obligated. Confirm at fincen.gov/boi before concluding no BOI filing is due. If it applies it is a FILING and is never public — it does not affect the founder-anonymity constraint on the website.
requirements.where_it_lands: Non-website: FinCEN filing determination

requirements.requirement: SCOPE HOLE — commission before finalizing the privacy policy: this analysis is US-only, and the US surface is thin, but the company's actual data-protection exposure is Moroccan (Law 09-08 / CNDP, which requires notification or authorization filings for processing AND for cross-border transfers) and European (GDPR — Art. 3(1) establishment-by-servers is arguable given German VPSs, plus Art. 28 processor duties, Art. 30 records, and Art. 44-49 transfer rules), with WhatsApp message content as Art. 9-adjacent special-category-risk material. The privacy policy text is downstream of that analysis, not independent of it. Note also that seller-client DPAs will likely require SUBPROCESSOR DISCLOSURE with a notice/objection right — a contractual obligation that will force the vendor's name into a document even though no US website law does.

jurisdictions.findings:
## MOROCCO COMPLIANCE SURFACE — iGrowFast LLC (Wyoming) — verified against primary texts

All statutory text below was extracted from the actual PDFs (Bulletin Officiel / CNDP / Bank Al-Maghrib), not from secondary summaries. Where I could not verify, I say UNCERTAIN.

---

### 1. LOI 09-08 — TERRITORIAL SCOPE (the jurisdictional hook)

**Primary text:** https://www.cndp.ma/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/Loi-09-08-Fr.pdf (Dahir 1-09-15, 18 Feb 2009, BO n° 5714 du 05/03/2009)

09-08 is modelled on **EU Directive 95/46, NOT the GDPR**. This matters enormously: there is **no "targeting" or "monitoring" test** like GDPR Art 3(2). Morocco uses the older **"means/equipment" test**.

**Article 2-2 verbatim:**
> « 2- La présente loi s'applique au traitement des données à caractère personnel […] :
> a) Lorsqu'il est effectué par une personne physique ou morale dont le responsable est établi sur le territoire marocain. Le responsable d'un traitement qui exerce une activité sur le territoire marocain dans le cadre d'une installation, qu'elle que soit sa forme juridique, y est considéré comme établi ;
> b) Lorsque le responsable n'est pas établi sur le territoire marocain mais **recourt, à des fins de traitement des données à caractère personnel, à des moyens automatisés ou non, situés sur le territoire marocain**, à l'exclusion des traitements qui ne sont utilisés qu'à des fins de transit […] »

**Article 2-3 verbatim (the sting):**
> « 3- Dans le cas visé au b du paragraphe 2 ci-dessus, le responsable du traitement doit notifier à la Commission nationale, **l'identité d'un représentant installé au Maroc** qui sans préjudice de sa responsabilité personnelle, **se substitue à lui dans tous ses droits et obligations** résultant des dispositions de la présente loi […] »

**Analysis — two independent routes into Moroccan jurisdiction:**

**Route A (weaker, UNCERTAIN):** iGrowFast LLC directly under Art 2-2(b). Servers are in Germany, entity in Wyoming. The question is whether Moroccan sellers'/agents' **browsers and phones in Morocco** are "moyens situés sur le territoire marocain". Under the classic Directive 95/46 reading (Art 29 WP Opinion WP56, 2002), a user's terminal equipment — cookies, JS, local storage — **is** equipment in the country, which is exactly the doctrine 09-08 Art 2-2(b) copies. **UNCERTAIN** whether CNDP actually applies WP56 doctrine to SaaS; I found no published CNDP decision applying the equipment test to a pure foreign SaaS. But if it does, Art 2-3 makes a **Moroccan representative mandatory**, and that representative inherits **all** the controller's obligations personally.

**Route B (strong, near-certain, and the one that actually bites):** The **Moroccan sellers are controllers established in Morocco** under Art 2-2(a) — squarely in scope, no argument. iGrowFast is their **sous-traitant (processor)**. The consequence is not that iGrowFast escapes; it is that **every Moroccan seller-client is personally exposed** for using iGrowFast, because iGrowFast's architecture forces them into an undeclared transfer abroad (§4). CNDP enforces against the Moroccan-established controller. This is a **commercial** risk before it is a legal one: a CNDP enforcement wave against sellers makes iGrowFast the reason their clients got fined.

Do **not** rely on the Wyoming incorporation as a shield. The entity's nationality is irrelevant to Art 2-2(b), and irrelevant to Route B entirely. CNDP's own position is that processing carried out on Moroccan territory is caught "qu'elles soient la propriété d'une entité marocaine ou d'un donneur d'ordre étranger (sous-traitance, délocalisation, etc.)" — https://www.cndp.ma/loi-09-08/

**Enforcement precedent proving CNDP reaches foreign-connected operators:** CNDP publicly acted against **TLSCONTACT** (visa-application operator serving FR/IT/DE/UK/BE embassies) for transferring video surveillance images abroad **without notification** — hearing 6 Jan 2023, compliance deadline 28 Feb 2023, Articles 52 and 60 invoked, referral to competent authorities. https://www.lexisma.info/2023/02/27/infraction-a-la-loi-n-09-08-communique-de-la-cndp-suite-a-labsence-de-notification-dun-transfert-de-donnees-personnelles-a-letranger/

---

### 2. DÉCLARATION vs AUTORISATION — Article 12 verbatim

> « Article 12 — Sauf dispositions législatives particulières, le traitement de données à caractère personnel doit faire l'objet :
> **1- D'une autorisation préalable** lorsque les traitements concernent :
> a) Les données sensibles visées à l'alinéa 3 de l'article premier […]
> b) **l'utilisation de données à caractère personnel à d'autres fins que celles pour lesquelles elles ont été collectées** ;
> c) des données génétiques […]
> d) des données portant sur les infractions, condamnations ou mesures de sûreté […]
> e) **des données comportant le numéro de la carte d'identité nationale** de la personne concernée ;
> f) L'interconnexion de fichiers […] dont les finalités principales sont différentes.
> **2- D'une déclaration préalable dans les autres cas** »

**Procedure / cost / timing (CNDP official):** https://www.cndp.ma/formalites/ · https://www.cndp.ma/notifier-un-traitement/
- **Déclaration**: form **F211** (normale) or **F214** (simplifiée). **Récépissé issued within 24 hours.** CNDP may convert to authorization within 8 days if manifest risk.
- **Autorisation**: form **F112**. CNDP opinion within **2 months**, extendable once. Clock restarts if file incomplete.
- **Transfer abroad**: form **F118**. **2 months**, extendable once.
- **Cost: free.** Online declaration with CNDP is free. (No fee appears anywhere in CNDP's formalities pages; secondary sources confirm "la déclaration est gratuite".) The cost is the local representative/counsel, not the filing.
- **Can a foreign entity file?** The filing itself is not restricted by nationality, but Art 2-3 requires notifying **the identity of a representative installed in Morocco** where jurisdiction arises via Art 2-2(b). A Moroccan **establishment** is not required; a **representative** is — and that person "se substitue à lui dans tous ses droits et obligations", i.e. bears personal liability. In practice this is a Moroccan subsidiary employee, a local lawyer, or a specialist consultant.

**Which iGrowFast processing escalates to AUTORISATION (not mere déclaration):**
1. **Art 12-1(b) — repurposing → AUTORISATION.** Feeding end-customer data and **WhatsApp message content** to **Anthropic / OpenAI** for AI features is use "à d'autres fins que celles pour lesquelles elles ont été collectées". The data was collected to fulfil a COD order, not to train/infer. **This is the single most under-appreciated trigger in the stack.** It also carries criminal exposure under Art 54 (below), not just Art 52.
2. **Art 12-1(e) — CIN → AUTORISATION.** Moroccan COD/courier flows sometimes capture the *carte nationale d'identité* number at delivery. If any CIN field exists anywhere in the schema, the whole processing escalates. **Design rule: never store CIN.** This is cheap to avoid now and expensive later.
3. **Art 12-1(a) — sensitive data → AUTORISATION.** WhatsApp **message content** is free text. It will incidentally contain health, religious, and political data (pharmacy orders, religious-product sales, etc.). A COD platform processing raw message bodies cannot credibly assert it never touches sensitive data. **UNCERTAIN** how CNDP treats incidental sensitive data in unstructured content; there is no published Moroccan doctrine analogous to EDPB guidance. Flagging rather than asserting.
4. Note: **transfer abroad does NOT appear in the Art 12 autorisation list.** It has its **own separate regime** under Arts 43/44 (§4). Both apply cumulatively — you need the underlying déclaration/autorisation *and* the F118.

---

### 3. TRANSFERTS À L'ÉTRANGER — Arts 43/44 — THE CRITICAL EXPOSURE

**Article 43 verbatim:**
> « Le responsable d'un traitement ne peut transférer des données à caractère personnel vers un Etat étranger que si cet Etat assure un niveau de protection suffisant de la vie privée et des libertés et droits fondamentaux […] La Commission nationale établit la liste des Etats répondant aux critères […] »

**Article 44 verbatim (derogations):**
> « Par dérogation aux dispositions de l'article 43 ci-dessus, le responsable d'un traitement peut transférer des données à caractère personnel vers un Etat ne répondant pas aux conditions prévues à l'article ci-dessus, **si la personne à laquelle se rapportent les données a consenti expressément à leur transfert** ou :
> 1- Si le transfert est nécessaire : a) à la sauvegarde de la vie […] b) à la préservation de l'intérêt public ; c) […] défense d'un droit en justice ; **d) à l'exécution d'un contrat entre le responsable du traitement et l'intéressé**, ou de mesures précontractuelles […] e) à la conclusion ou à l'exécution d'un contrat conclu ou à conclure, **dans l'intérêt de la personne concernée**, entre le responsable du traitement et un tiers ; f) […] entraide judiciaire […] g) […] affections médicales.
> 2- Si le transfert s'effectue en application d'un accord bilatéral ou multilatéral auquel le Royaume du Maroc est partie ;
> **3- Sur autorisation expresse et motivée de la Commission nationale** lorsque le traitement garantit un niveau de protection suffisant […] **notamment en raison des clauses contractuelles ou règles internes** dont il fait l'objet. »

**ADEQUACY LIST — verified from the primary deliberation:**
Délibération n°236-2015 du 18 décembre 2015 (modifying n°465-2013): https://www.cndp.ma/wp-content/uploads/2023/01/deliberation-n-236-2015-18-12-2015.pdf

> « **Sous réserve de notifier à la CNDP, suivant le régime approprié, tout transfert de données à caractère personnel vers l'étranger** […] la Commission considère que les pays suivants offrent un niveau de protection suffisant […] :
> **Allemagne**, Autriche, Belgique, Bulgarie, Canada, Chypre, Danemark, Espagne, Estonie, Finlande, France, Grèce, Hongrie, Irlande, Islande, Italie, Lettonie, Liechtenstein, Lituanie, Luxembourg, Malte, Norvège, Pays-Bas, Pologne, Portugal, République Tchèque, Roumanie, Royaume-Uni, Slovaquie, Slovénie, Suède, Suisse. »

**→ GERMANY IS ADEQUATE. THE UNITED STATES IS NOT ON THE LIST.**

This is the decisive asymmetry, and it cuts **against** the entity's own nationality:

**(a) German VPSs (Contabo) — the easy half.** Germany is adequate under Art 43. The substance is fine. **But adequacy does NOT remove the notification duty.** The deliberation's own chapeau conditions the whole list on "**Sous réserve de notifier à la CNDP […] tout transfert**". CNDP's website-compliance guide is explicit that hosting abroad is a transfer requiring a filing: « **Une demande de transfert à l'étranger en cas d'hébergement et de stockage des données personnelles sur des serveurs situés à l'étranger.** » CNDP's *notifier-un-traitement* page states the F118 is required and that "l'autorisation de transfert à l'étranger d'un fichier de données personnelles n'est accordée que lorsque le traitement sous-jacent a fait l'objet d'une demande de déclaration ou d'autorisation approuvée par la CNDP."
**Tension flagged honestly:** CNDP's *notifier-une-demande-de-transfert* page reads as though adequate-list transfers flow freely. That reading conflicts with the deliberation chapeau and the website guide. **The safe and defensible position: file the F118 for Germany.** It is free, takes 2 months, and the substance is uncontroversial because Germany is listed. There is no rational reason to litigate this. **UNCERTAIN only as to whether omission would be enforced; not uncertain that filing is correct.**

**(b) The USA — the hard half, and it is structural, not incidental.**
The USA is **absent** from the list. Every one of these is a transfer to a non-adequate state:
- **iGrowFast LLC itself** — a Wyoming entity. Any admin/support access from the US to Moroccan personal data **is a transfer to the USA**. The company's own nationality *creates* the violation. This is the inversion the founders should understand: being American is a liability here, not a shield.
- **Anthropic, OpenAI** — US processors of customer data and WhatsApp content.
- **Meta (WhatsApp), TikTok, Snapchat, Google Analytics, Meta Ads, Shopify** — US recipients.

**Which Art 44 gateway is actually available?** Work it honestly:
- *Consentement exprès* — **practically unavailable for end-customer data.** The sellers' customers never interact with iGrowFast. Consent must be **express**, and it must be to the **transfer** specifically. You cannot bootstrap it from the seller's T&Cs. Dead end at scale.
- *Art 44-1(d)* — "contrat entre le responsable du traitement et l'intéressé". For the **seller** as controller, the sale contract with the customer exists, so a transfer *necessary to execute delivery* is arguable. But this **collapses for AI processing**: sending message content to Anthropic/OpenAI is not *necessary* to execute the sale. Nor is Meta Ads. "Necessary" is a strict test, not a convenience test.
- *Art 44-1(e)* — "dans l'intérêt de la personne concernée" with a third party — arguable for the courier leg only.
- **→ *Art 44-3* — express, reasoned CNDP authorization on the basis of contractual clauses / internal rules. This is the only route that actually covers the US leg of this architecture.** It is the Moroccan analogue of SCCs/BCRs, but unlike the GDPR, **you cannot self-serve** — SCCs are not a self-executing instrument in Morocco. **CNDP must expressly authorize, in a reasoned decision.** 2 months, extendable once.

**Penalty for transferring without it — Article 60 verbatim:**
> « Est puni d'un **emprisonnement de trois mois à un an** et d'une **amende de 20.000 à 200.000 DH** ou de l'une de ces deux peines seulement, quiconque effectue un transfert de données à caractère personnel vers un Etat étranger, en violation des dispositions des articles 43 et 44 de la présente loi. »

**Article 64 doubles fines for legal persons** → **40.000–400.000 MAD** for the company, **and the directors remain personally exposed to the prison term** ("sans préjudice des peines qui peuvent être appliquées à ses dirigeants"). Art 64 also permits **confiscation partielle des biens**. Art 61 permits the court to order **effacement de tout ou partie des données** — i.e. deletion of the production database.

**Blunt assessment:** the fines are small (400k MAD ≈ USD 40k). **The fines are not the risk.** The risks are (i) personal criminal liability of directors, (ii) a deletion order against the production dataset, (iii) CNDP's public naming register (live since 31 March 2023), and (iv) contamination of the seller base, who are the ones with Moroccan assets to seize. Do not price this as a fine.

---

### 4. PENALTIES UNDER 09-08 — full verbatim schedule (Chapitre VII)

Criminal, not administrative. All amounts MAD. **Art 64 doubles every fine where the offender is a legal person, and directors are separately liable.**

| Art | Conduct | Penalty |
|---|---|---|
| 52 | Operating a file **without déclaration/autorisation** (Art 12); or continuing after withdrawal of récépissé | **10.000–100.000 DH** (no prison) |
| 53 | Refusing access / rectification / opposition rights (Arts 7,8,9) | **20.000–200.000 DH par infraction** |
| 54 | Fraudulent/unfair/unlawful collection; **processing for purposes other than those declared/authorized**; incompatible further processing | **3 mois–1 an** + **20.000–200.000 DH** |
| 55 | Retention beyond declared/legal duration | **3 mois–1 an** + **20.000–200.000 DH** |
| 56 | Processing in violation of Art 4 (consent) | **3 mois–1 an** + **20.000–200.000 DH** |
| 57 | Sensitive data without express consent | **3 mois–1 an** + **50.000–300.000 DH** |
| 58 | Failure to implement security measures (Arts 23, 24) | **3 mois–1 an** + **20.000–200.000 DH** |
| 59 | Processing despite opposition, incl. **prospection commerciale / électronique** (Arts 9, 10) | **3 mois–1 an** + **20.000–200.000 DH** |
| **60** | **Transfer abroad violating Arts 43/44** | **3 mois–1 an** + **20.000–200.000 DH** |
| 61 | Controller/**sous-traitant**/staff who, **even by negligence**, cause or facilitate misuse or disclose to unauthorized third parties | **3 mois–1 an** + **20.000–200.000 DH** + court may order **saisie du matériel** and **effacement des données** |
| 62 | Obstructing CNDP inspection; refusing documents | **3–6 mois** + **10.000–50.000 DH** |
| 63 | Refusing to apply CNDP decisions | **3 mois–1 an** + **10.000–100.000 DH** |
| 64 | **Legal person** → **fines doubled**; + possible **confiscation partielle des biens** | — |

Note **Art 61 expressly names the *sous-traitant*.** iGrowFast's processor status does **not** insulate it. Negligence suffices.

---

### 5. IS THERE A NEWER LAW? — reform status

**No. Loi 09-08 remains in force and is the operative law as of July 2026.** A reform aligning Morocco with the GDPR (legal bases, accountability, sanction levels, a posteriori control replacing heavy a priori filing) has been under discussion for **several years**, driven by CNDP president **Omar Seghrouchni**, but **no text has been adopted**. Sources consistently report **no definitive text adopted as of April 2026**. I could **not** identify a *projet de loi* number, a Conseil de gouvernement adoption, or a Bulletin Officiel publication. **UNCERTAIN as to any bill number or parliamentary stage — I will not invent one.**

**Planning implication:** do not defer compliance waiting for the reform. The reform's direction (lighter a priori filing, heavier a posteriori sanctions) would, if anything, **increase** exposure for an architecture that never filed. https://www.cndp.ma/loi-09-08/ · https://telquel.ma/sponsors/legislation-faire-evoluer-la-loi-09-08-pour-mieux-nous-proteger_1904757

---

### 6. WHAT MUST APPEAR ON THE WEBSITE — CNDP's own guide

**Primary:** *Lignes directrices relatives à la conformité des sites web à la loi 09-08* — https://www.cndp.ma/wp-content/uploads/2023/01/CNDP-guide-conformite-sites-web-fr.pdf

CNDP requires the site to inform users of: identity of the controller, purpose, recipients, whether replies are obligatory or optional, the existence of access/rectification/opposition rights, the service where those rights are exercised, **and — verbatim — « le numéro du récépissé de la déclaration ou de l'autorisation délivré par la CNDP »**.

**CNDP's model clause (clause type), verbatim, to be placed in "conditions générales"/"mentions légales":**
> « ……….(indiquer l'identité du responsable du traitement qui exploite le site)
> Les informations recueillies sur le site www……… font l'objet d'un traitement destiné à……….(préciser la finalité)
> **Les destinataires des données sont :………..(préciser)**
> Conformément à la loi n° 09-08 promulguée par le Dahir 1-09-15 du 18 février 2009 […] vous bénéficiez d'un droit d'accès et de rectification aux informations qui vous concernent, que vous pouvez exercer en vous adressant à :………(préciser une adresse, un mail ou un service…).
> Vous pouvez également, pour des motifs légitimes, vous opposer à ce que les données qui vous concernent fassent l'objet d'un traitement.
> **Ce traitement a été notifié et autorisé par la CNDP au titre du récépissé / de l'autorisation n°……… du …/…/….** »

**Model short mention for collection forms:**
> « Conformément à la loi 09-08, vous disposez d'un droit d'accès, de rectification et d'opposition au traitement de vos données personnelles. Ce traitement a été autorisé par la CNDP sous le n°…. »

Also mandated by the guide:
- **Cookies (§10):** consent **before** deposit of cookies involving personal data; state the purpose; explain how to object. GA/Meta Ads/TikTok/Snap pixels are all caught.
- **Consent checkbox must NOT be pre-ticked** ("La case d'acceptation ne doit pas être pré-cochée").
- **Prospection directe (§9):** prior consent at collection, **or** the person previously received an analogous product/service from the same controller. **Every** marketing message must carry a phone number, email, or other unsubscribe mechanism, free of charge. → **WhatsApp broadcast campaigns are prospection directe.** Art 59 criminalizes sending despite opposition: 3 mo–1 yr + 20k–200k (doubled → 400k). For a WhatsApp-centric COD product this is a live, recurring, per-message risk — arguably more likely to generate a complaint than the transfer issue, because recipients notice it.
- **Security (§7)** and **sous-traitance**: the guide requires choosing a processor giving sufficient guarantees **and** a **contract or legal act** binding processor to controller. → iGrowFast **must** have a written DPA with each seller-client. Today it likely does not.
- **Proportionality (§6)** and **retention limited to purpose (§8)**.

**Nothing in 09-08 requires publishing the EIN, and nothing requires publishing founder names.** Both constraints are fully satisfiable. The CNDP model clause requires the **identity of the controller** — that is the **legal entity** ("iGrowFast LLC", Wyoming Filing ID 2026-002024077, 30 N Gould St Ste R, Sheridan, WY 82801), **not** any natural person. Publish the entity, its address, and a rights-exercise contact. Founder names and EIN stay off.

### 7. **"MESSAGING INFRASTRUCTURE PROVIDERS, EU-HOSTED" — is the generic category sufficient?** (direct answer)

**Split answer. The constraint holds in one place and fails in two.**

- **On the public website / privacy notice — PROBABLY SUFFICIENT, but weaker than you think.** CNDP's model clause says « Les destinataires des données sont :………..(**préciser**) ». *Préciser* means *specify*, not *categorize*. A generic category is a **defensible market-practice position**, not a clearly compliant one. **UNCERTAIN** — I found no CNDP decision accepting or rejecting category-level recipient disclosure. Risk is low and tolerable.
- **On the F118 transfer filing — NOT SUFFICIENT. Hard blocker.** The F118 requires the **destination** and the **recipient identity**, plus the contractual clauses or internal rules relied on, and (where applicable) references to the foreign authority's approval. You **cannot** file "a category". CNDP cannot assess adequacy against an unnamed vendor in an unnamed country. **The vendor must be named to the regulator.** This is not public disclosure — the filing is not the website.
- **In the DPA with seller-clients — NOT SUFFICIENT.** The CNDP guide obliges the controller (the seller) to choose a processor giving sufficient guarantees. A seller cannot discharge that duty against an unnamed sub-processor, and cannot make their own F118 filing without knowing the destination. Sophisticated sellers will refuse to sign.

**Reconciliation that respects the constraint:** keep the generic category on the **public** page; name the vendor in (i) the **F118 filing** and (ii) the **DPA / sub-processor annex** furnished to seller-clients under NDA. Public genericity and regulatory specificity are not in conflict — they are different audiences. **Note EU-hosting is favourable here:** an EU host is on the adequacy list, so naming it is *cheap* — the substance passes Art 43 trivially. The instinct to conceal is costing you nothing legally and buying nothing legally; it is purely a commercial preference, and it should not be allowed to block the filing.

### 8. LOI 31-08 (CONSUMER PROTECTION) — the surprise: it does NOT bind your refund policy

**Primary text:** Loi 31-08, dahir 1-11-03 du 18 février 2011, BO n°5932 du 07/04/2011 — https://www.onssa.gov.ma/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/Reglementation/C.Reglementation-Connexe/4.%20Divers/LOI.31-08.FR.pdf

**Article 2 verbatim — the definition that decides it:**
> « On entend par **consommateur** toute personne physique ou morale qui acquiert ou utilise pour la satisfaction de ses **besoins non professionnels** des produits, biens ou services qui sont destinés à son **usage personnel ou familial**.
> Le **fournisseur** est défini comme toute personne physique ou morale qui agit dans le cadre d'une activité professionnelle ou commerciale. »

**→ iGrowFast's own subscribers are e-commerce sellers and companies — professional use. They are NOT "consommateurs". Loi 31-08 does NOT govern iGrowFast's SaaS refund policy.** The 7-day withdrawal and 15-day refund rules **do not apply to iGrowFast's own subscription terms.** iGrowFast is contractually free to set its refund policy (subject to general contract law / DOC and unfair-terms doctrine as between merchants). **This directly contradicts the naive reading and the secondary sources — resolve it in your favour, but resolve it deliberately, not by accident.**

**Where 31-08 DOES land: on your sellers, and therefore on your product's feature surface.**

**Article 36 verbatim (withdrawal):**
> « Le consommateur dispose d'un délai :
> - **de sept jours** pour exercer son droit de rétractation ;
> - **de trente jours** pour exercer son droit de rétractation, **si le fournisseur n'honore pas son engagement de confirmer par écrit les informations** prévues dans les articles 29 et 32.
> Et cela, sans avoir à se justifier, ni à payer des pénalités, à l'exception, le cas échéant, **des frais de retour**.
> Les délais […] courent à compter de la **date de réception du bien** ou de l'acceptation de l'offre pour les prestations de services. »

**Article 37 verbatim (refund) — resolves the 15-vs-30-day conflict in the secondary sources:**
> « Lorsque le droit de rétractation est exercé, le fournisseur est tenu de rembourser, **sans délai**, au consommateur le **montant total payé** et **au plus tard dans les 15 jours** suivant la date à laquelle ce droit a été exercé. **Au-delà, la somme due est, de plein droit, productive d'intérêts au taux légal en vigueur.** »

**The "30 days" circulating in secondary sources is wrong** — 30 days is the *extended withdrawal* window under Art 36 when written confirmation was not honoured, **not** the refund deadline. The refund deadline is **15 days**, and late refunds accrue statutory interest automatically ("de plein droit").

**Article 38 exclusions** (no withdrawal right): services begun with consent before the 7 days elapse; price tied to financial-market fluctuations; **goods made to consumer specification or clearly personalised, or which by nature cannot be returned or spoil rapidly**; audio/video/software unsealed by the consumer.

**Article 29 — cyber-commerçant mandatory pre-contract disclosures** the seller must show: identity/legal form/siège social; **RC number and capital**; **IF (numéro d'identité fiscale)** if VAT-registered; licence number if regulated; delivery times and costs; **existence of the Art 36 withdrawal right**; payment/delivery/performance terms; offer validity; cost of the distance-communication technique; minimum contract duration where applicable.

**Article 35:** « Les opérations de paiement relatives aux contrats conclus à distance sont soumises à la législation en vigueur. Le fournisseur garantit au consommateur la sécurité des moyens de paiement qu'il propose. »

**Product consequence:** iGrowFast's order/return model must be able to represent a **7-day (or 30-day) rétractation window distinct from the courier's "retour" status**, and a **15-day refund clock with interest accrual**. Given the existing "retour livré" / UNPAID-on-delivery return-leg semantics, a rétractation is **not** the same event as a carrier return — conflating them will misstate sellers' legal position and mis-time the 15-day clock. This is a data-model requirement, not a policy paragraph.

### 9. LOI 53-05 / LOI 43-20 — electronic signatures & e-exchange

- **Loi 53-05** (échange électronique de données juridiques, dahir 1-07-129 du 30 novembre 2007) — https://www.cndp.ma/images/lois/loi-53-05-echange-electronique-donnees-juridiques-fr.pdf · https://www.dgssi.gov.ma/en/loi-53-05-relative-lechange-electronique-de-donnees-juridiques
- **Loi 43-20** (services de confiance pour les transactions électroniques) **partially repealed 53-05** — specifically the **chapitre préliminaire and Titre II** of 53-05. The portions of 53-05 on the **validity of acts in electronic form** survive. 43-20 covers electronic signature/seal validation and preservation, electronic time-stamping, electronic registered mail, and **website authentication**. DGSSI FAQ: https://www.dgssi.gov.ma/sites/default/files/publications/pdf/2024-09/FAQ_related_to_law_43-20_v1.1_in_french.pdf

**Relevance to iGrowFast: low, and do not manufacture it.** These matter only if the product asserts that something is a **legally binding signed instrument** — e-signed seller contracts, signed proof-of-delivery with evidential weight, certified timestamps. Ordinary click-accept T&Cs and app-recorded COD confirmations do **not** require a qualified signature; they are ordinary evidence. **Do not claim "signature électronique" or "horodatage certifié" in marketing** unless using a 43-20-qualified trust service provider — an unqualified claim is both a consumer-law misrepresentation risk and undermines the very evidential value being asserted. **UNCERTAIN** on 43-20's precise entry-into-force date; one source states 13 July 2013, which is plainly wrong (predates the law) and appears to be an OCR/typo artifact. Do not rely on that date.

### 10. COD & PAYMENT LICENSING (BANK AL-MAGHRIB) — the existential question, answered

**Primary text:** Loi n° 103-12 relative aux établissements de crédit et organismes assimilés (dahir 1-14-193 du 24 décembre 2014) — https://www.bkam.ma/en/content/download/757666/8545663/loi%20bancaire%20fr%2022.pdf

**Article 15 verbatim:** « Les établissements de paiement sont ceux qui offrent un ou plusieurs services de paiement visés à l'article 16 ci-après. »

**Article 16 verbatim — the decisive test:**
> « **1) Sont considérés comme services de paiement :**
> - **les opérations de transfert de fonds** ;
> - les dépôts et les retraits en espèces sur un compte de paiement ;
> - **l'exécution d'opérations de paiement par tout moyen de communication à distance, à condition que l'opérateur agisse uniquement en qualité d'intermédiaire entre le payeur et le fournisseur de biens et services** ;
> - l'exécution de prélèvements permanents ou unitaires, d'opérations de paiement par carte et l'exécution de virements, lorsque ceux-ci portent sur des fonds placés sur un compte de paiement.
> On entend par **compte de paiement** tout compte détenu au nom d'un utilisateur de services de paiement et qui est exclusivement utilisé aux fins d'opérations de paiement.
> **2) Ne sont pas considérés comme services de paiement**, les opérations de paiement effectuées par : un chèque […] une lettre de change […] un mandat postal émis et/ou payé en espèces ; tout autre titre similaire sur support papier. »

**Article 17 verbatim (segregation, if licensed):**
> « Les fonds inscrits dans les comptes de paiement doivent être déposés sur un **compte global, séparé et individualisé** auprès d'un établissement de crédit habilité à recevoir des dépôts à vue. Ces fonds doivent être distinctement identifiés et **cantonnés** dans la comptabilité des établissements de paiement. Le solde de ce compte ne peut faire l'objet d'un droit résultant de créances propres […] ni d'aucune saisie-arrêt par les créanciers […] »

**Article 35-2 verbatim (legal form):** « Les établissements de paiement sont constitués sous forme de **société anonyme ou de société à responsabilité limitée**. »

**Article 183 verbatim — THE PENALTY:**
> « Est punie d'un **emprisonnement de six (6) mois à trois (3) ans** et d'une **amende de 100.000 à 5.000.000 de dirhams** ou de l'une de ces deux peines seulement, toute personne qui :
> - **exerce, à titre de profession habituelle, les opérations visées aux articles 1 et 16 ci-dessus sans avoir été dûment agréée** en tant qu'établissement de crédit ;
> - effectue des opérations pour lesquelles elle n'a pas été agréée. »

Art 182 additionally punishes (3 mo–1 yr + 20k–200k) anyone who uses naming/advertising **suggesting** they are licensed or who maintains public confusion about the regularity of their activity — **this is a marketing-copy constraint**, see below.

**THE BRIGHT LINE — apply it honestly:**

**SAFE (no agrément needed): iGrowFast as a system of record.** If the platform only **records, computes, reconciles, and reports** COD amounts — the courier collects the cash from the end-customer, the courier remits to the seller, and **no money ever enters an iGrowFast-controlled account** — then iGrowFast performs **no** Art 16 service. It is bookkeeping software. Commission calculations, payout *statements*, seller_payments ledgers, and "pay_seller" RPCs that record an obligation are **accounting entries, not payment operations**. This is the current posture implied by the ledger/statement architecture, and it is defensible.

**FATAL (agrément required): the moment funds flow through iGrowFast.** If iGrowFast ever (a) receives COD proceeds from couriers into its own account and remits to sellers, (b) nets its commission out of collected cash before remitting, or (c) holds seller balances that sellers can draw down — that is **"opérations de transfert de fonds"** and **"intermédiaire entre le payeur et le fournisseur de biens et services"** under Art 16, performed *à titre de profession habituelle*. → **Art 183: 6 months–3 years imprisonment + 100.000–5.000.000 MAD.**

Note the severity gap: **the banking penalty is an order of magnitude worse than the entire data-protection schedule** — 3 years vs 1 year, 5M MAD vs 400k. This, not CNDP, is the genuinely existential item.

**And iGrowFast LLC structurally cannot cure it.** Art 35-2 requires an établissement de paiement to be a **société anonyme or SARL** — **Moroccan corporate forms**. A **Wyoming LLC is neither**. Obtaining an agrément would require **incorporating a Moroccan subsidiary (SA/SARL)**, meeting BAM's minimum capital (set by circular du wali), submitting business plan, shareholder/manager identities, and compliance/risk arrangements, and passing BAM review. Morocco has ~18 licensed payment establishments (Cash Plus, Wafacash, NAPS, M2T, Chari Money, etc.). **This is a 12–24 month, capital-intensive regulatory project — not a feature.** (**UNCERTAIN** on the exact minimum capital figure, which is fixed by circular rather than in 103-12 itself; and I did not verify a categorical bar on foreign *shareholding* of a Moroccan SA/SARL — foreign ownership of the Moroccan subsidiary is generally permissible; the bar is on the *Wyoming LLC itself* holding the licence.)

**Operating rules that follow — treat as architectural invariants:**
1. **Never let COD cash touch an iGrowFast account.** Courier → seller directly. iGrowFast invoices the seller **separately** for SaaS/commission, out of band. The instant commission is netted from collected COD, you are unlicensed money transmission.
2. **Never let sellers hold a withdrawable balance** on the platform. A "balance you can cash out" is a *compte de paiement* in substance regardless of what the schema calls it. The existing ledger is safe **only** while it records obligations rather than custodies funds.
3. **Marketing copy is a legal surface (Art 182).** Do not say "we pay your sellers", "wallet", "payouts", "we collect your COD", "escrow", "iGrowFast Pay". Say "we **track**, **reconcile** and **report** COD collected by your carrier". The existing internal vocabulary ("payouts", "pay_seller", "seller_payments") is fine **internally**; it must not become external positioning. Art 182 punishes maintaining public confusion about the regularity of the activity — a "wallet" UI is exactly that.
4. Art 16-2 note: cash **mandats postaux** and paper instruments are carved out. Not a workaround for a platform.
5. **Chèque/traite carve-out does not help** an app-mediated cash flow.

### 11. PRIORITY ORDER (blunt)

1. **Never touch COD cash.** Free to comply with today; catastrophic and unfixable-by-a-US-LLC if breached. Art 183.
2. **File the déclaration (F211) + F118 for Germany.** Free, 24h/2mo, substance uncontroversial (Germany is listed). Removes the Art 52/60 predicate and the seller-contamination risk.
3. **Confront the US leg (Art 44-3).** iGrowFast's own American nationality, plus Anthropic/OpenAI/Meta/Google, are transfers to a non-adequate state with **no available derogation at scale**. This needs an express, reasoned CNDP authorization on contractual clauses. It is the hardest item and the one most likely to be ignored.
4. **AI features are an Art 12-1(b) autorisation trigger + Art 54 criminal exposure**, not a déclaration. Do not ship AI over customer/WhatsApp content on a bare declaration.
5. **WhatsApp broadcast = prospection directe** (Art 59, CNDP guide §9). Consent + unsubscribe in every message. Highest complaint probability of anything here.
6. **Put the CNDP récépissé number on the site** once obtained, with the model clause; cookie consent not pre-ticked.
7. **Sign DPAs with seller-clients** naming sub-processors (CNDP guide §7 requires a contract). Generic categories fail here and in F118 — but succeed on the public page.
8. **Never collect CIN.** Escalates everything to autorisation for no benefit.
9. **31-08 does not bind your SaaS refund policy** (Art 2 — professional use). It binds your sellers; your data model must carry a 7/30-day rétractation window distinct from carrier "retour", and a 15-day refund clock accruing statutory interest.
10. **EIN and founder names**: nothing in Moroccan law requires either. Publish the **entity** as controller. Constraint fully satisfiable.
