requirements.requirement: File the underlying déclaration préalable (form F211 normale, or F214 simplifiée) with CNDP before processing. Récépissé issued within 24 hours; filing is FREE. CNDP may convert it to an authorization within 8 days if it identifies manifest risk. This is the prerequisite for the F118 transfer filing ('l'autorisation de transfert à l'étranger n'est accordée que lorsque le traitement sous-jacent a fait l'objet d'une demande de déclaration ou d'autorisation approuvée par la CNDP') and for the récépissé number the website must display. Art 52 penalizes operating a file without it at 10,000-100,000 MAD (doubled to 200,000 under Art 64).
requirements.where_it_lands: Non-website: CNDP regulatory filing — the first domino; everything else sequences off it

requirements.requirement: Loi 31-08 does NOT bind iGrowFast's own SaaS refund policy. Art 2 defines 'consommateur' as acquiring for 'besoins non professionnels' and 'usage personnel ou familial' — e-commerce sellers and companies are professional users and are NOT consumers. The 7-day withdrawal (Art 36) and 15-day refund (Art 37) rules therefore do not constrain iGrowFast's subscription terms, which remain free (subject to general contract law/DOC and unfair-terms doctrine between merchants). Do not import consumer-law language into the refund policy by reflex — but make this an explicit, documented decision rather than an accident.
requirements.where_it_lands: Website: refund policy / terms of service — a freedom to exercise deliberately, not an obligation

requirements.requirement: The order/return data model must represent a rétractation window (7 days from receipt of goods under Art 36; extended to 30 days if the seller did not honour written confirmation of Art 29/32 information) as an event DISTINCT from a carrier 'retour' status, plus a 15-day refund clock from exercise of the right, after which the sum accrues statutory interest 'de plein droit' (Art 37). Conflating rétractation with the existing 'retour livré' / carrier-return semantics will misstate sellers' legal position and mis-time the 15-day clock. Art 38 exclusions apply (personalised goods, goods that spoil, unsealed software/audio/video, services begun with consent before the 7 days elapse).
requirements.where_it_lands: Non-website: order/return data model and status semantics — a schema requirement, not a policy paragraph. Loi 31-08 binds the SELLERS, and the product must be capable of supporting their compliance.

requirements.requirement: Do not claim 'signature électronique', 'horodatage certifié', or legally-binding signed proof-of-delivery in marketing or product copy unless using a Loi 43-20 qualified trust service provider. Loi 43-20 (services de confiance pour les transactions électroniques) partially repealed Loi 53-05 — specifically its chapitre préliminaire and Titre II — while the 53-05 provisions on validity of acts in electronic form survive. Ordinary click-accept T&Cs and app-recorded COD confirmations do NOT require a qualified signature; they are ordinary evidence. An unqualified claim is both a misrepresentation risk and self-defeating (it undermines the evidential value being asserted). UNCERTAIN: one source states a 13 July 2013 entry-into-force for 43-20, which is plainly wrong (predates the law) and appears to be an OCR artifact — do not rely on it.
requirements.where_it_lands: Website: product/features copy; and non-website: proof-of-delivery architecture if evidential weight is ever asserted

requirements.requirement: Do not defer compliance pending Moroccan data-protection reform. Loi 09-08 remains in force and is the operative law as of July 2026. A GDPR-alignment reform (legal bases, accountability, sanction levels, lighter a priori filing in exchange for stronger a posteriori control) has been under discussion for years under CNDP president Omar Seghrouchni, but no text has been adopted — no projet de loi number, no Conseil de gouvernement adoption, and no Bulletin Officiel publication could be identified (UNCERTAIN; I will not invent a bill number). The reform's direction would if anything INCREASE exposure for an architecture that never filed.
requirements.where_it_lands: Non-website: compliance sequencing and planning assumption

platforms.findings:
## SCOPE NOTE ON SOURCES

Everything below is from official Meta/WhatsApp properties. Two caveats on evidence quality, stated up front so you don't over-trust a line:

- Several `facebook.com/business/help/*` pages (notably the canonical **Display name guidelines**, ID `757569725593362`, and **About Business Verification**, ID `1095661473946872`) are JS-rendered and return only a title to a fetcher. Their substance below is reconstructed from Meta's own search-surfaced snippets and from the developer-docs pages that normatively reference them. Where a rule rests on a snippet rather than full page text, I mark it **[snippet-sourced]**.
- `whatsapp.com/legal/commerce-policy` and `business.whatsapp.com/policy` now 301 to `whatsappbusiness.com`. The Commerce Policy no longer enumerates its own prohibited list — it delegates to the **Meta Commerce Policy**. I could not retrieve the Meta Commerce Policy enumeration itself (`transparency.meta.com/policies/commerce-policies/` 404s; Community Standards exposes it only as "Restricted Goods and Services"). The messaging-side prohibited list IS retrieved and authoritative, and it is the one that actually gates you.

---

## 1. APP REVIEW — REQUIRED FIELDS

Source: [Privacy Policy Expectations](https://developers.facebook.com/docs/development/terms-and-policies/privacy-policy/), [App Dashboard](https://developers.facebook.com/docs/development/create-an-app/app-dashboard/), [Become a Tech Provider](https://developers.facebook.com/docs/whatsapp/solution-providers/get-started-for-tech-providers/).

Basic Settings carries the review-gating fields: **category, platform, icon, Privacy Policy URL, Terms of Service URL, Data Deletion**.

**App Icon (hard spec):** < 5 MB, between 512×512 and 1024×1024 px, JPEG/GIF/PNG.

**Category:** must accurately describe the app. For iGrowFast the honest fit is Business/Productivity — *not* "Messaging" (see §9; claiming a messaging identity compounds the brand problem).

**Privacy Policy — what reviewers actually check.** This is the single most mechanically enforced item, and it is checked by crawler, not goodwill:
- Live at an **active, publicly available, easily accessible** URL, returning **HTTP 200** (they test via the Sharing Debugger).
- **Not geo-blocked.** This is a live risk for you: if any edge rule, Cloudflare geo-gate, or WAF challenge fronting the marketing site blocks US datacenter IPs or serves an interstitial to Meta's crawler, the submission fails. Meta reviewers and crawlers hit from outside Morocco. Test the policy URL from a US IP and with a generic bot UA before submitting.
- Links **live, clickable, accessible to Meta's crawlers** — so the policy must be server-rendered HTML, not text painted by client-side JS behind a hydration gate.
- Page **clearly marked as a privacy policy**.
- Policy must **belong to your company, not another organization** — it must say *iGrowFast LLC*, not a template's residual name.
- "**Broken privacy policy links are considered violations and are subject to enforcement.**" Enforcement here means app restriction, not just rejection.

**Minimum privacy-policy content Meta requires:** (a) what information you collect, directly and via third parties, including automatically-collected data (browser, server, usage); (b) how you process it and the purpose; (c) **a clear way for users to request deletion of their data**, via email or contact form, and the contact method must be current and functional.

That third element is the hinge between §1 and §2 — Meta requires the deletion route *in the policy text itself*, independent of the Basic Settings URL field.

**Tech Provider adds two videos** to the submission: (1) sending a message through your app to WhatsApp, (2) creating a message template. And: *"If they are unable to access your app to test it, your entire submission will be rejected."* A marketing site with a login wall and no reviewer credentials is a rejection. Supply test credentials.

---

## 2. DATA DELETION — EXACT SPEC

Source: [Data Deletion Callback](https://developers.facebook.com/docs/development/create-an-app/app-dashboard/data-deletion-callback).

Meta's FAQ is explicit that it is an **either/or**: *"Developers need to specify either a data deletion callback instruction URL or a callback URL found in Basic Settings for your app."*

**Option A — Callback URL (programmatic).** Must: use **HTTPS**; be registered in the App Dashboard **"Data Deletion Request URL"** field; **initiate deletion of all app data about the user from Facebook**; and **return JSON** shaped exactly:
```
{ "url": "<status_url>", "confirmation_code": "<alphanumeric_code>" }
```
The returned `url` must give the user *"a human-readable explanation of the status of their request, including a legitimate justification for any refusal to delete."* Note that clause — a refusal is permitted **only with a stated lawful justification** (e.g. tax retention). It is not a licence to ignore.

**Option B — Instructions URL (the owner's "request delete data" page).** This is the correct choice for iGrowFast: the callback is designed around Facebook Login user IDs, which you don't use. Meta does **not** publish a content spec for the instructions page — this is a genuine documentation gap, and anyone who tells you there's an official checklist is inventing it. The defensible spec is the *union* of what Meta does specify elsewhere (privacy-policy expectations + callback semantics), which is what reviewers pattern-match against:

The page must: be public, no login required, 200, not geo-blocked, crawlable, permanently addressed (e.g. `/data-deletion`); **state deletion is available**; give a **step-by-step method** (a form and a named mailbox, e.g. `privacy@igrowfast.com`, monitored — Meta requires the contact be *functional*, and they do test it); state **what gets deleted and what is retained with the lawful justification and retention period** (this mirrors the callback's "legitimate justification for any refusal"); state a **turnaround SLA**; describe **identity verification** for the requester; and — critical for your architecture, see §4 — **route end-customer requests to the seller (controller), not to iGrowFast**.

**The structural trap.** Your product holds two populations: (i) your users — sellers, media buyers, couriers (you are **controller**); (ii) the sellers' end customers — names, phones, delivery addresses, order contents, **WhatsApp message content** (you are **processor**). A single "delete my data" button cannot serve both: you have **no lawful authority to unilaterally delete a seller's customer records** on that customer's say-so — that is the seller's call as controller, and doing it yourself would breach both your Art. 28 instructions and the seller's own records-retention duties. The page must therefore fork explicitly: *"If you are an iGrowFast account holder → [this route]. If you are a customer of a business that uses iGrowFast → we process your data on that business's behalf; contact them; if you cannot identify or reach them, contact us at X and we will route your request to them and support their response."* That fork is also what proves to a GDPR-literate reviewer that you understand your own role — its absence is the single most common tell of a copy-pasted policy.

---

## 3. BUSINESS VERIFICATION — AND THE WEBSITE MATCH

Source: [Become a Tech Provider](https://developers.facebook.com/docs/whatsapp/solution-providers/get-started-for-tech-providers/), [About Business Verification](https://www.facebook.com/business/help/1095661473946872) **[snippet-sourced]**, [Required documents for registered entities](https://www.facebook.com/business/help/193400874040813) **[snippet-sourced]**.

**Sequencing is a hard gate:** *"Your business must be verified before you can start the app review process."* Verification is not parallel to review — it precedes it. Budget for it.

Meta requires: **business name, address, phone number, email, and website**; confirmation of your connection to the business; and supporting documents. For incorporated/registered entities: **tax identification number, proof of identity, and a business formation document**.

**Does the website need to show the legal entity name and address? — Direct answer: YES, in substance.**

The mechanism, stated precisely so you can act on it: **website is itself a submitted verification field**, and verification is an exercise in **cross-corroboration** — Meta matches the entity on your formation document against independently observable signals, and your public site is the signal they control least and therefore weight heavily. Your evidence set is:
- **Legal name:** `iGrowFast LLC`
- **Formation doc:** Wyoming Filing ID `2026-002024077`, filed 07/07/2026, Active
- **Address:** 30 N Gould St Ste R, Sheridan, WY 82801

If the site says only "iGrowFast" with no legal entity and no address, while the documents say "iGrowFast LLC, Sheridan WY", the reviewer has **nothing to match on** and rejection risk is high — this is the top cause of avoidable verification failure.

**Do this:** put `iGrowFast LLC`, the full Sheridan address, and a contact email in the **site footer** and on **Terms, Privacy, and Contact**. Registered-agent addresses at 30 N Gould St are extremely well known to reviewers as a mass-registration address, which does **not** disqualify you but **does** mean every other signal must be clean and consistent — so make the match trivially easy rather than clever.

**Two absolute constraints, both compatible with the above:**
- **EIN: never on the website.** Correct instinct, and there is no tension — the EIN is uploaded *in the verification flow*, never published. Meta never requires a public tax ID.
- **Founder names: never on the website.** Also compatible. Meta requires *"confirmation of your connection to the business"* and *proof of identity* — but that is **submitted privately in the verification flow** (and a Wyoming LLC does not publicly list members). Nothing in Meta's verification requires a public founder name. Keep the site entity-level: legal name + address + entity role, no natural persons.

**One honest caveat.** Verification also weighs whether the business appears **operationally real** — a site that is only a logo and a waitlist form corroborates nothing. The site must show the actual product, a coherent description of what the company does, and working legal pages. That is a substance requirement, not a founder-disclosure requirement.

---

## 4. META PLATFORM TERMS — TECH PROVIDER OBLIGATIONS

Source: [Meta Platform Terms](https://developers.facebook.com/terms/dfc_platform_terms/).

- **Purpose limitation + segregation.** Process Platform Data **solely for your clients' purposes**; keep different clients' data **segregated**; do not use it for your own ends. This is a genuine constraint on the AI roadmap: feeding client WhatsApp message content to Anthropic/OpenAI **for your own model improvement or cross-client features is a breach**. Per-client inference, on that client's instruction, is fine.
- **Deletion (§3.d.i.2.d):** *"you must… delete all Platform Data as soon as reasonably possible"* on client request or when the client stops using the service. Your retention schedule must have a WhatsApp-data path that actually fires — not just an intent.
- **Sub-processing (§5.a.i.1):** written agreements with every service provider requiring them to *"use the Platform and Process Platform Data only for you and according to your instructions."* You remain **responsible for subcontractors' compliance**. This binds your EU messaging-infrastructure provider, Contabo, R2, and every LLM vendor.
- **Onward transfer** is closed-list: to your client; where law requires (retain proof); to your own service providers as necessary; to the client's service providers **only if the client expressly requests**. Nothing else.
- **Privacy policy (§4.b):** must explain *"which data you Process, how you Process it, the purposes for which"*, plus **how users request deletion**; and it **must not contradict Meta's terms**. Meta enforces §4.f violations against live apps — this is not theoretical.

**What must land in your customer terms:** mirror Meta's restrictions downward — purpose limitation, no discriminatory processing, no surveillance use, deletion-on-request, sub-processor flow-down, and an explicit statement that for end-customer data **the seller is controller and iGrowFast is processor acting on documented instructions**. You need a **DPA**, not just a ToS.

**Jurisdiction reality — the part that will bite you regardless of Meta.** Wyoming incorporation does not buy you out of the EU. Infrastructure in **Germany (Contabo)** = processing **in the Union** → **GDPR Art. 3(1) establishment-based applicability**, which is the strongest hook there is and does not care where you're incorporated. Morocco-centric users additionally implicate **Law 09-08 / CNDP**. Message **content** processing raises the stakes: content is the highest-sensitivity tier, and Art. 32 security + Art. 28 instruction-fidelity are both live. You are also making **onward transfers to US LLM vendors (Anthropic/OpenAI)** — Chapter V transfer machinery (SCCs) applies, and Platform Terms independently constrain those transfers.

**The generic-processor-category question — regime by regime, because the answer differs and this is exactly where people get it wrong:**
- **Public privacy policy under GDPR: a generic category is SUFFICIENT.** Art. 13(1)(e) requires *"the recipients **or categories of recipients**"* — categories are expressly permitted by the text. **"Messaging infrastructure providers (EU-hosted)" is lawful on the public site.** Your constraint holds here.
- **Your DPA with seller-clients: a generic category is NOT sufficient.** Art. 28(2)–(3)(d) requires controller authorisation of sub-processors and prior notice of changes — which is **operationally impossible against an unnamed vendor**, since a controller cannot object to a change it cannot see. EDPB guidance and standard practice require the sub-processor **list be made available to the controller**. Resolution: keep the public site generic, and **name the vendor in the DPA / a linked sub-processor list available to contracted clients**. That satisfies both your confidentiality preference and Art. 28. Do not let the public-site constraint leak into the DPA — that is the actual legal exposure.
- **Meta Platform Terms: silent on public naming**, but demands the written flow-down (§5.a.i.1) regardless. Category-only disclosure does not discharge it.

---

## 5. MESSAGING + COMMERCE POLICY — IS COD FINE?

Source: [WhatsApp Business Messaging Policy](https://whatsappbusiness.com/policy/).

**Prohibited industries (retrieved, authoritative):** firearms/weapons; alcohol; tobacco (limited country exceptions); prescription drugs, recreational and other drugs; **medical products and health services**; endangered species; live non-endangered animals (except livestock); hazardous goods and materials; real/virtual/counterfeit currencies incl. ICOs and binary options; body parts or organic fluids; **fraudulent or deceptive business models**; real-money gambling (limited exceptions); adult products and services; **dating services**; **multi-level marketing**; payday loans, salary advances, peer-to-peer lending, debt collection, bail services. Plus: no discrimination or suggested preference based on personal characteristics (ethnicity, religion, gender, sexual orientation, disability, medical condition).

**COD verdict — direct answer: COD is NOT prohibited.** The policy **does not address payment method at all**. Prohibition attaches to the **product being sold** and the **conduct of the messaging**, never to how the buyer pays. General e-commerce is permitted where the business complies with Meta's Commerce rules and applicable law. Nothing in the retrieved policy touches cash-on-delivery.

**Where the real risk sits — and it is not COD, it is your merchant base.** You are a platform; Meta will judge you substantially by **what your sellers push through your integration**. Two named prohibitions are precisely aimed at the failure modes endemic to COD/dropshipping in the Morocco/MENA market:
- **"Fraudulent or deceptive business models"** — the standard COD-dropshipping pathologies (product materially unlike the ad, invented "medical" or slimming claims, fake urgency, undisclosed identity) land squarely here.
- **"Medical products and health services"** — flatly prohibited, and this is the highest-probability enforcement event for you. Slimming products, supplements, "herbal" remedies, sexual-wellness items and cosmetic-medical devices are **staples of Moroccan COD catalogues** and are **prohibited outright**. If your sellers message about them via your integration, you absorb the enforcement.
- **Opt-in is mandatory:** the recipient must have given their number **and** given opt-in permission. In COD workflows the number arrives via a landing-page order form — **an order is not a marketing opt-in**. Order-status messages are serviceable; promotional blasts to that number without separate consent are not. Meta's stated best practice is **per-category consent** with clear opt-out.

**Actionable:** your seller ToS/AUP must prohibit these categories by name and reserve suspension rights, and you need real enforcement capability. "Our customers did it" is not a defence — §4 makes you responsible.

---

## 6. BRAND / TRADEMARK — GATES THE DEMO SECTION

Source: [WhatsApp Brand Guidelines](https://www.meta.com/brand/resources/whatsapp/whatsapp-brand/), [WhatsApp IP Policy](https://www.whatsapp.com/legal/ip-policy).

Baseline: you may use WhatsApp trademarks **only as expressly permitted by the Brand Guidelines, or with prior written permission**. This is permissive-by-exception, not permissive-by-default.

**Prohibited:**
- Any use **implying partnership, sponsorship, or endorsement** — verbatim: *"ÉVITER d'utiliser les Ressources de marque WhatsApp d'une façon qui sous-entend une forme de partenariat, de parrainage ou de soutien."* **This is the rule that governs you right now, because you are pre-approval.**
- **Combining** the WhatsApp name or logo with any other logo, company name, mark, or generic term. So: no "iGrowFast for WhatsApp" lockup, no logo mashups, no `WhatsApp + iGrowFast` sandwich graphic.
- Using WhatsApp Brand Resources **in the name of a non-WhatsApp product or service**.
- **Modifying the logos**, including recolouring: *"It is forbidden to modify the colors of our logos."*
- Using an image that **too closely resembles the WhatsApp phone glyph**.

**Required when you do refer to it:** capitalise **W** and **A** — "WhatsApp". Never "Whatsapp", "WHATSAPP", or "WA". Use only official assets from Meta's brand centre.

**Answering the three questions asked, precisely:**

**"Can we say 'WhatsApp'?"** — **Yes.** Nominative/descriptive reference to accurately describe your subject matter is the guidelines' own carve-out (they grant it explicitly for books/plays, *"as long as it's clear that WhatsApp doesn't endorse or sponsor your project"*). So **"Works with WhatsApp"** / **"WhatsApp integration"** as a plain factual capability statement is defensible. **"WhatsApp-Powered Inbox"** as a product name is not — that is brand-in-product-name.

**"Can we show the logo?"** — **Practically, no; don't.** The guidelines don't grant third parties a general marketing licence to display the logo, and the book/play carve-out **explicitly withholds it**: you may use the word, but *"you may not use WhatsApp logos or images… without prior written permission."* Combined with the no-combining rule, putting the glyph on your landing page next to your own logo is the highest-risk asset on the site. Use the **word mark in text**. Ship the site without the glyph.

**"Can we show a WhatsApp-looking inbox UI?"** — **This is your real exposure, and the honest answer is that the guidelines do not squarely address screenshots** — I'm not going to manufacture a rule. What they *do* prohibit is dispositive by application: no implied endorsement, no unmodified-asset misuse, no phone-glyph lookalikes. A pixel-faithful WhatsApp-chrome clone — WhatsApp green `#25D366`, the glyph, WhatsApp's bubble geometry and header — **implies endorsement and reproduces protected trade dress**, and does so on the very page a Meta reviewer will open while deciding whether to trust you. Compounding it: showing a fake WhatsApp UI while **not yet approved** is the exact "conveys a relationship that doesn't exist" pattern.

**Build the demo in your own design language.** Show *your* product's inbox — your colours, your typography, your chrome — which is what you're actually selling and is 100% safe. Convey the WhatsApp connection with a **text label** ("WhatsApp conversations, in one inbox"), not by cloning their interface. This costs you nothing commercially and removes the review risk entirely.

**Disclaimer.** No specific attribution text is mandated by the guidelines — do not invent an "official" one. Since the operative requirement is that non-endorsement **be clear**, a plain footer line discharges it:
> *"WhatsApp is a trademark of WhatsApp LLC, registered in the U.S. and other countries. iGrowFast LLC is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by WhatsApp LLC or Meta Platforms, Inc."*

Note that disclaimer becomes **false once you are an approved Tech Provider** — diarise the revision.

---

## 7. TIERS — AND WHICH FITS

Source: [Solution Providers overview](https://developers.facebook.com/docs/whatsapp/solution-providers/), [Become a Tech Provider](https://developers.facebook.com/docs/whatsapp/solution-providers/get-started-for-tech-providers/).

| Tier | What it is | Gate |
|---|---|---|
| **Direct Cloud API** | Own use only, not a partner | Own app; no partner review |
| **Tech Provider** | Full services to clients; **no credit line** — clients add their own payment method, Meta bills clients for API, you bill for your services | Business verification → App Review → Advanced access to both permissions |
| **Solution Partner** | Full services **plus credit lines** (clients need no payment method), direct invoicing, SMB Accelerator eligibility | **Meta Business Partner status first**, then Solution Partner qualification. Described as *"most complex and lengthy."* Not an open self-serve application |
| **Tech Partner** | Tech Provider upgraded to Meta Business Partner status | Start as Tech Provider, then apply |

Both Tech Provider and Solution Partner require the **same** advanced permissions: `whatsapp_business_messaging` (send on clients' behalf) and `whatsapp_business_management` (access clients' WABAs).

**Which fits iGrowFast — direct answer: Tech Provider.** It is the only tier realistically open to you: Solution Partner requires Meta Business Partner status first, which a 2026-incorporated LLC will not clear. Tech Provider gives you the identical permission set and identical technical capability — the **only** thing you forgo is the credit line, i.e. your sellers each attach their own payment method and Meta bills them directly. For a COD-seller base that is arguably *better*: you never front messaging spend or carry your customers' credit risk. Path is then **Tech Provider → (later, with traction) Tech Partner**. There is also an interim option the docs flag: onboard **under an existing Solution Partner** by supplying their app ID — worth considering if you need to ship before your own review clears.

---

## 8. DISPLAY NAME / VERIFIED NAME

Source: [Display names](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/business-messaging/whatsapp/display-names), [Display name guidelines](https://www.facebook.com/business/help/757569725593362) **[snippet-sourced]**, [About creating a business name](https://faq.whatsapp.com/793641088597363) **[snippet-sourced]**.

- Display name is **auto-verified against the guidelines**; on failure status is `DECLINED`; appeal via Developer Support.
- Must be **related to the business** and not violate WhatsApp Commerce and Business policies.
- **Cannot contain any variation of the word "WhatsApp."** Absolute. This forecloses any client-facing number named "iGrowFast WhatsApp", and reinforces §6's product-naming rule.
- Cannot be **all capitals** or use **extra spaces** — single spacing only. Exception: businesses that already brand that way externally may match their external branding (capitalisation/punctuation) — **which is exactly why the website matters**: your site *is* the evidence of external branding, so "iGrowFast" must appear consistently there.
- **Change limit:** max 3 changes in the first 30 days; then a 30-day wait.
- Display-name approval is a prerequisite for **Official Business Account** (green badge) status.

---

## 9. PROHIBITED MARKETING CLAIMS PRE-APPROVAL

**"Can we market 'WhatsApp integration' before approval?"** — **Yes, factually; but with real limits, and one of them is honesty about tense.**

Permitted: descriptive, accurate capability statements — *"Works with WhatsApp"*, *"WhatsApp integration"*, *"Manage your WhatsApp conversations"* — carrying the non-endorsement footer, with correct **WhatsApp** casing, and no logo.

Prohibited pre-approval (any of these can sink review, since the reviewer reads the site):
- **"Official WhatsApp Partner" / "Meta Partner" / "Meta Business Partner"** — all false today. Partner badges are earned and licensed; using one unearned is both a brand violation and a misrepresentation. **This is the claim most likely to appear on a founder-written landing page — kill it now.**
- **"WhatsApp-approved", "Certified", "Endorsed by Meta"** — same.
- Any **logo lockup** implying partnership (§6's no-combining rule).
- **WhatsApp in the product name** — "iGrowFast WhatsApp Suite" (§6 + §8).
- **Cloned WhatsApp UI** implying you *are* WhatsApp (§6).

**The accuracy point you should not skip.** Your memory-of-record shows messaging today runs through a **third-party messaging infrastructure provider (Evolution API)** — i.e. **not** the official Cloud API. So *"WhatsApp integration"* is true, but *"built on the WhatsApp Business Platform"*, *"official Cloud API"*, or *"official WhatsApp API"* would be **false today** and would be false **on the very site a Cloud API reviewer opens while assessing you**. That is a self-inflicted wound: a reviewer who sees an unapproved applicant already claiming official-API status reads it as either misrepresentation or evidence of unofficial-access use — the latter being an independent basis for denial. Keep the site to capability claims until Cloud API access is actually granted, then upgrade the copy and drop the disclaimer in the same edit.

---

## PRIORITY ORDER

1. **Footer/legal-page entity block** (`iGrowFast LLC` + Sheridan address) — gates §3, cheapest fix, highest rejection-avoidance.
2. **Kill any "Official/Certified Partner" claim and the WhatsApp logo/UI clone** — gates §6/§9, and it is what the reviewer sees first.
3. **`/data-deletion` page with the controller/processor fork** — gates §1/§2 and demonstrates §4 literacy.
4. **Privacy policy rewrite** — 200, crawlable, un-geo-blocked, deletion route in-text, iGrowFast-named.
5. **Business verification submitted and cleared** — blocks App Review entirely; start it first in wall-clock terms.
6. **Seller AUP naming prohibited categories** (medical/slimming especially) + DPA naming the sub-processor to clients.

requirements.requirement: Publish the legal entity name "iGrowFast LLC" and full registered address (30 N Gould St Ste R, Sheridan, WY 82801, USA) so it matches the Wyoming formation document (Filing ID 2026-002024077) submitted to Meta. Website is itself a submitted verification field; reviewers cross-corroborate the site against the formation document. No founder names needed; identity proof is submitted privately in the verification flow.
requirements.where_it_lands: Website footer (site-wide) + Terms of Service + Privacy Policy + Contact page

requirements.requirement: NEVER publish the EIN. Tax ID is uploaded inside the Meta verification flow only; Meta never requires a public tax identifier.
requirements.where_it_lands: Non-website action: Meta Business Verification document upload

requirements.requirement: Complete Business Verification BEFORE starting App Review — it is a hard sequential gate: "Your business must be verified before you can start the app review process." Requires business name, address, phone, email, website, confirmation of your connection to the business, plus tax ID, proof of identity, and business formation document.
requirements.where_it_lands: Non-website action: Meta Business Suite verification (start first in wall-clock terms)

requirements.requirement: Privacy Policy URL must be live, publicly accessible, return HTTP 200, NOT be geo-blocked, be crawlable by Meta's crawlers (server-rendered HTML, not JS-hydrated), be clearly marked as a privacy policy, and belong to iGrowFast LLC (not a residual template name). Test from a US IP with a generic bot UA — Cloudflare/WAF geo-gates or interstitials fronting the site will fail the check. Broken links are violations subject to enforcement, not just rejection.
requirements.where_it_lands: Website /privacy + Meta App Dashboard Basic Settings field

requirements.requirement: Privacy policy must state: (a) what information is collected, directly and via third parties, including automatically-collected data (browser, server, usage); (b) how it is processed and the purpose; (c) a clear way for users to request deletion of their data via email or contact form, with a contact method that is current and functional (Meta tests it).
requirements.where_it_lands: Website /privacy

requirements.requirement: Provide EITHER a Data Deletion Callback URL OR a Data Deletion Instructions URL in Basic Settings. Choose the Instructions URL: the callback is built around Facebook Login user IDs, which this product does not use.
requirements.where_it_lands: Meta App Dashboard Basic Settings + website /data-deletion

requirements.requirement: The /data-deletion page must fork by data-subject role: iGrowFast account holders (sellers/media buyers/couriers — company is CONTROLLER) get a direct deletion route; end-customers of sellers (company is PROCESSOR) are directed to the seller as controller, with iGrowFast offering to route the request. A single undifferentiated delete button is unlawful — iGrowFast has no authority to unilaterally delete a seller's customer records and doing so would breach Art. 28 instructions and Platform Terms purpose-limitation.
requirements.where_it_lands: Website /data-deletion

requirements.requirement: The /data-deletion page must be public (no login), 200, un-geo-blocked, permanently addressed, and must state: deletion is available; step-by-step method (form + monitored mailbox e.g. privacy@igrowfast.com); what is deleted vs retained WITH the lawful justification and retention period; turnaround SLA; requester identity-verification method. (Meta publishes no official content spec for the instructions page — this is the defensible union of the privacy-policy expectations and the callback's "legitimate justification for any refusal to delete" semantics.)
requirements.where_it_lands: Website /data-deletion

requirements.requirement: Remove any "Official WhatsApp Partner", "Meta Partner", "Meta Business Partner", "WhatsApp-approved", "Certified", or "Endorsed by Meta" claim. All are false pre-approval and are both brand violations and misrepresentation — and the reviewer reads the site while deciding.

Use the word mark in text only.

requirements.requirement: Do NOT build a pixel-faithful WhatsApp-chrome clone for the demo (WhatsApp green #25D366, phone glyph, WhatsApp bubble geometry/header). Guidelines do not squarely address screenshots, but the no-implied-endorsement rule, the no-logo-modification rule, and the prohibition on "an image that resembles too closely the WhatsApp telephone logo" apply. platforms.findings:
## SCOPE NOTE / CONFIDENCE

Everything below is from official docs fetched 2026-07-16. Three items I could NOT fully verify and flag as **VERIFY**: (1) TikTok Business Products (Data) Terms — `ads.tiktok.com/i18n/official/policy/business-products-terms` is behind a login wall; (2) TikTok Shop Partner Center Developer ToS + data-security review — `partner.tiktokshop.com` served truncated content; (3) Snap's full Brand Guidelines PDF (rules live in a downloadable PDF at snap.com/brand-guidelines, not in HTML). Do not treat my TikTok-Shop and Snap-logo conclusions as final without pulling those three.

---

## THE THREE FINDINGS THAT ACTUALLY THREATEN THE BUSINESS MODEL

These are not website copy issues. They are product/contract conflicts. Address before writing a single line of the Shopify listing.

### 1. Shopify PPA §9.14(2)(ii) — the partner may not contact the merchant's customers. **This is aimed straight at your WhatsApp COD-confirmation product.**

Verbatim, from https://www.shopify.com/partners/terms:

> "Partner will not communicate with Customers directly or indirectly, provided however that Partner may contact Customers if the information is obtained from another source, such as from the Customers themselves"

With definitions:
> "'Customer' means any individual that visits or transacts via the Merchant Store."
> "'Merchant Data' means information (including personal information) relating to a Merchant, including but not limited to business, financial and product information and any Customer Data."

Your core loop is: pull the order → get the end-customer's phone → WhatsApp them to confirm the COD order. If the phone number came from the Shopify order, that is Merchant Data, and messaging that person is exactly "communicate with Customers … indirectly." The carve-out ("obtained from another source, such as from the Customers themselves") does not save you when the number originates in the Shopify order object.

The defensible structure — and it must be built into the product, not just asserted in a policy — is that the **merchant** is the sender: the message goes out over the merchant's own WhatsApp identity, initiated by the merchant's own staff/agent, with iGrowFast acting only as the conduit under a DPA. Automated/bulk sends triggered by iGrowFast on the merchant's behalf are the grey zone. Get this in writing from Shopify Partner support before the app review, not after. Severity: **blocking** for the Shopify app specifically. Zero website impact — the fix is architecture + contract.

### 2. Shopify PPA — absolute ban on AI/ML training with Merchant Data or Customer Data. You integrate Anthropic and OpenAI.

> "Developers are prohibited from using, or enabling third parties to use, Merchant Data and Customer Data … to create, develop, train, fine tune, or improve any machine learning or artificial intelligence systems"

…absent explicit written consent from Shopify (or the merchant, for merchant-specific data). Note "**or enabling third parties to use**." Inference is not training, and both Anthropic and OpenAI's API defaults are no-training/zero-retention — but the burden is on you to (a) confirm you're on no-training API terms, not consumer tiers, (b) disclose AI sub-processing in the privacy policy, and (c) state affirmatively that customer data is never used to train models. That last sentence should appear on your privacy policy verbatim; it's cheap and it defuses the reviewer's first question.

### 3. WooCommerce Vendor Agreement §1.2.9 / §1.2.10 — you may not price on payment volume, nor offer payment processing.

From https://woocommerce.com/woo-vendor-agreement/:
- §1.2.9: vendor cannot collect "revenue based on the total value of payments completed using the Product"
- §1.2.10: vendor cannot offer "a solution for processing or enabling payment transactions" without a separate agreement

A COD platform whose pricing is a % of collected cash, or which handles seller payouts/remittance, trips both. Your existing product does run seller payouts (`pay_seller`, payout ledger). For the Woo Marketplace listing specifically, the pricing model must be flat/seat/tier-based, and the listed extension should be scoped to order-sync + messaging, with payout/remittance living outside the marketplace product. Severity: **blocking** for Woo Marketplace only. Lands on pricing page + product scoping.

---

## SHOPIFY

### Website / listing gate
Mandatory listing fields (https://shopify.dev/docs/apps/launch/shopify-app-store/app-store-requirements, .../privacy-requirements, .../distribution/support-your-customers):
- **Privacy policy URL** — "you must provide a privacy policy and link to it from your Shopify App Store listing." Applies to full AND limited-visibility apps. Non-negotiable.
- **Support email** — "All public apps are required to provide at least one support channel." Email is always required even if it's not your preferred channel. Optional additions: support portal URL, display-only phone number.
- **Emergency developer contact** in the Partner Dashboard.
- Test credentials + a screencast of onboarding.

Shopify's own recommended privacy-policy contents (from privacy-requirements): data collected via Shopify APIs; data from merchants; data from merchants' customers; how it's used; **retention periods**; **geographic location and data processing/storage locations**; how merchants can contact you. That "geographic location" line is why your Germany/Contabo hosting must be on the page — a US-LLC-badged site that is silent on EU hosting reads as a mismatch to a reviewer.

### Listing content prohibitions (all real rejection reasons)
- "Your app and app listing should only include factual information." No statistics/data, no "unsubstantiated claims such as guarantees."
- **No reviews or testimonials in the listing.** (Your marketing site may have them; the Shopify listing may not.)
- **No pricing information in images**, or anywhere outside the designated pricing section.
- Name must "lead with your distinctive brand identifier" and must not be confusingly similar to another app.
- No "import from any store in the world"-style marketing claims.
- No capital funding / loans / cash advances. (Relevant if you ever front COD cash to sellers — that would be an app-store disqualifier.)
- **Billing must go through Shopify App Pricing or the Billing API** for all app charges, and merchants must be able to upgrade/downgrade "without having to contact your support team."

### Mandatory compliance webhooks (https://shopify.dev/docs/apps/build/compliance/privacy-law-compliance)
Required for every App Store app **regardless of whether the app collects personal data**. Subscribe via `shopify.app.toml` before submission. All three: POST, JSON body, `Content-Type: application/json`, must verify Shopify HMAC header, **reject invalid signatures with 401**, acknowledge valid ones with a 200-series code.

| Topic | Payload | Obligation |
|---|---|---|
| `customers/data_request` | `shop_id`, `shop_domain`, `orders_requested[]`, `customer{id,email,phone}`, `data_request{id}` | Provide the requested customer data **to the store owner** within **30 days** |
| `customers/redact` | `shop_id`, `shop_domain`, `customer{id,email,phone}`, `orders_to_redact[]` | Erase within **30 days**, or supply legal justification for retention. Timing: sent 10 days after the request if the customer hasn't ordered in 6 months; otherwise withheld until 6 months pass |
| `shop/redact` | `shop_id`, `shop_domain` | Sent **48 h after uninstall**. Erase all data for that shop |

Product obligation this creates for you: an erasure path that reaches **every** store of end-customer data — Postgres rows, WhatsApp `messages`/media in R2, the blind-HMAC keyword search index (mig 067a/067b), backups/logical dumps, and anything sitting in Anthropic/OpenAI logs. The HMAC search index is the sneaky one: it's derived from message plaintext, so redaction must purge index entries too, not just source rows. Your R2 preflight ordering rule (media orphaning — see the conversation-cleanup edge fn) is the same class of trap here.

Separately, API License (https://www.shopify.com/legal/api-terms) requires deletion within **30 days** when "the Merchant uninstalls the Application, [or] it is no longer required to provide the services," and breach notice to Shopify "immediately upon, but no later than twenty-four (24) hours."

### Protected customer data (https://shopify.dev/docs/apps/launch/protected-customer-data)
Reading name/address/phone/email on an order = protected customer data fields = **Level 1 + Level 2 both apply**. You will read all four.

Level 1: process only the minimum personal data; inform merchants what you process and why; limit processing to stated purposes; respect customer consent; respect opt-outs from data sharing/"data sale"; allow opt-out of automated decision-making with legal/significant effects; **make privacy and data protection agreements with your merchants**; apply retention periods; encrypt at rest and in transit.

Level 2: encrypt backups; keep test and production data separate; data loss prevention strategy; limit staff access; strong passwords for staff accounts; **keep an access log to protected customer data**; security incident response policy.

Three of these are live gaps against your known stack: (a) "keep test and production data separate" — the `test env` business with 300 seeded orders lives in the prod DB; that will be asked about. (b) "keep an access log to protected customer data" — audit-log was deliberately ripped out on 2026-06-22 for perf reasons; Level 2 wants it back, at least scoped to protected-customer-data reads. (c) "encrypt your data backups" — verify against the R2 backup design.

### Brand / trademark
Sources: PPA §5 (https://www.shopify.com/partners/terms), https://www.shopify.com/legal/trademarks, https://help.shopify.com/en/partners/partner-program/shopify-branding, https://shopify.dev/docs/apps/launch/marketing/shopify-brand-assets.

Permitted: "display the Shopify Trademarks solely as necessary to perform Partner's obligations" and "for the sole purpose of notifying Merchants that the Application or Theme is compatible with the Service." So a plain-text factual compatibility statement — "Shopify integration", "Works with Shopify" — is within the stated purpose. Ideally hyperlink the mention to shopify.com (trademarks page: name/brand-asset mentions "should ideally include an embedded hyperlink").

Prohibited:
- Shopify marks (or variations/misspellings) in "Partner's business name, logo, branding, advertising, social media or domain name." → no `shopify.igrowfast.com`, no "Shopify" in the app name, no Shopify glyph in your logo lockup.
- Buying "search engine or other pay-per-click keywords … trademarks, email addresses or domain names that use the Shopify Trademarks." You must **add "Shopify" as a phrase-match negative keyword** to your keyword campaigns. That's an affirmative marketing-ops task, not a website one.
- "Shopify Partner" badge/tier badges: only if you actually hold the status; logos "must not be altered in any way," cannot be translated, cannot be folded into your own logo; badge updates within 48 h of tier change.
- The only officially blessed logo asset for app marketing is the **Shopify App Store Ad Badge**, min 30px height, unaltered, and "where used on a web page, the Badge should include embedded hyperlinks to your app listing page on the Shopify App Store."
- Partnership implication: API terms state "The parties … are independent contractors. Neither party is an agent, representative or related entity of the other party." Don't imply endorsement.

Domains that ARE allowed per the branding page: `igrowfast.com/shopify` and `shopify.igrowfast.com`… note the branding help page permits "Shopify subdomains under your brand: shopify.partnername.com" while PPA §5 bars Shopify marks in a domain name. These conflict on their face. **Take the conservative read: use `igrowfast.com/shopify` (path, not subdomain).**

### Other Shopify prohibitions worth knowing
- Cannot "develop an Application whose primary purpose is to migrate Merchants off of Shopify."
- Cannot "use the Shopify API to substantially replicate products or services offered by Shopify."
- No fake reviews or false purchase notifications; no auto-adding or pre-selecting optional charges without explicit buyer consent; no promotions/ads in admin extensions; no apps connecting merchants to agencies/freelancers.
- Asking for reviews must use neutral language; no incentives, no withholding features for reviews; no collecting reviews "through the app or external channels."

---

## WOOCOMMERCE

### Gate
Sources: https://developer.woocommerce.com/docs/woo-marketplace/submitting-your-product/, https://woocommerce.com/woo-vendor-agreement/, https://woocommerce.com/document/marketplace-support-guidelines/, https://woocommerce.com/document/marketplace-privacy/.

Four review phases: **business review** (product fit + a revenue-share business model + competitive pricing), **code review** (original, secure, PHP 7.4+, current WC/WP), **UX review** (WordPress Accessibility Coding Standards, block editor, **HPOS compatibility mandatory for all new submissions**), **launch preparations**. Revenue share is 70/30 in the vendor's favour.

Website-side: a **privacy policy URL** ("A link to the privacy policy on your website") is a listing field. Note the submission doc itself only names product .zip / business details / testing instructions as "critical details" — the privacy-policy URL requirement surfaces in the listing fields and the vendor agreement, not the submission guide. Don't read the submission guide as exhaustive.

Support: **email only**, through Woo's support system. Woo handles live chat and routes product-specific queries to your support email. Obligations: timely email responses, handling reviews/ratings promptly, managing feature requests on product pages. Per §1.1.11 you must "provide Product support to Users in accordance with the Woo Support Guidelines."

### Data / privacy
§1.1.1: "provide clear and conspicuous notice to potential and existing Users of any terms and conditions that the Partner requires Users to agree to." → your ToS must be linked from the listing and reachable, not buried.
§1.1.8: "provide all notices, and obtain all consents, required under applicable law in connection with Partner's collection, use and sharing of any personally identifiable information collected by Partner via the Product" — and you may not "provide such data to information brokers."

Woo does **not** impose Shopify-style compliance webhooks, retention deadlines, or a levelled security program. It defers wholesale to applicable law + your own privacy policy. Practically: WooCommerce is the lightest gate of the four, and your GDPR posture is doing all the work.

### Brand / trademark — the strictest of the four
https://woocommerce.com/trademark-guidelines/:
- **"You may not use the WooCommerce and Woo logos for any purpose"** absent an approved trademark license. → **No Woo logo on your website.** This is the one place where "we'll just show their logo like everyone else" is flatly wrong.
- "Never use or incorporate WooCommerce or any Woo Mark as part of your brand, company, product, service or feature names."
- Use the mark "in plain text, non-stylized format (and not logo format)."
- Required phrasing pattern: "Use your distinctive product name immediately preceding the use of '**compatible with WooCommerce**' or '**for WooCommerce**'." → "iGrowFast for WooCommerce" ✅ / "WooCommerce COD Manager" ❌.
- Domains: avoid "WooThemes"/"WooCommerce" in domain names, or "Woo" "in a way that suggests an affiliation to Automattic."
- Required attribution when using Woo Marks: "**[insert Woo Mark] and its associated designs are trademarks of Automattic Inc.**" ← this exact string lands in your website footer / legal notices page.
- No suggesting Automattic/WooCommerce "has somehow sponsored, endorsed, or is otherwise affiliated with you."
- Vendor Agreement §1.2.2: cannot claim the Product is an "official" WordPress.com / WooCommerce product.
- Note: "Any open-source licenses on software released by Automattic cover copyright only, and do not include any express or implied right to use Automattic trademarks." GPL ≠ trademark rights.

WordPress.org plugin-directory naming convention (https://make.wordpress.org/plugins/2015/10/05/guidelines-for-plugins-that-include-company-andor-product-names-in-the-plugin-name/): the company name may not lead the slug. "Product Addons for WooCommerce" permitted; "WooCommerce – Product Addons" not.

### Listing prohibitions
- "exclude spam links, affiliate links, or links to upsell products outside of the Woo Marketplace."
- §1.2.3: cannot "display any link that leads to a third party site on Partner Page."
- §1.2.5 **price parity**: "The Product price on the Marketplaces must be the same as the fee charged for the Product outside of Marketplaces." → your public pricing page and the Woo listing price must match exactly. Real constraint on running promos on your own site.
- §2.3: Woo handles "User requests or claims related to returns, cancellations, refunds, and/or fraud" — so your own refund policy must not contradict Woo's for marketplace-sourced purchases.

---

## TIKTOK

### Website gate — the most website-specific of all four
https://developers.tiktok.com/doc/app-review-guidelines:

> "Your Privacy Policy and Terms of Service links must be visible on the website URL without having to open a menu to view them, and the links must be active."

Concretely: **footer links, always rendered, not behind a hamburger, not behind an accordion, not JS-gated.** On a mobile viewport a collapsed nav that hides the footer links is a rejection. And: the site must be "a fully developed, externally-facing website—not a landing page or login page." A single-page marketing splash or a bare login screen fails. This alone dictates that iGrowFast needs a real multi-page public site before a TikTok app is even submittable.

Also required: **URL ownership verification** for the app config (https://developers.tiktok.com/doc/getting-started-create-an-app#verify_url_ownership) — Privacy Policy and ToS URLs both. And "Provide mechanisms for users to contact you directly, and promptly address their concerns" → a real support contact page.

Demo video: up to 5 videos, ≤50 MB each, showing "the complete end-to-end flow of the up-to-date integrations," demonstrating every requested product and scope, at the exact URL/app you declared; sandbox environment for first-time approval.

Rejection triggers: still in development/testing; private or personal use; requesting unnecessary permissions beyond actual needs; unclear/incomplete integration in the demo.

For the Business/Marketing API specifically, expect Business Center onboarding, sandbox→production review, **business registration documents** for higher-volume access, and a data-security compliance audit covering privacy policy, data handling, storage, and consent mechanisms.

### App naming
"Must be custom and authentic," "shouldn't reference social media companies," should match your actual app/website name rather than describing functionality, and "must adhere to the TikTok Brand and Use Guidelines." App icon must not be "easily confused with another well-known brand icon."

→ The TikTok app must be named **iGrowFast**, not "TikTok Ads Manager for COD" or similar.

### Data obligations
Developer ToS (https://www.tiktok.com/legal/page/global/tik-tok-developer-terms-of-service/en):
> "a complete and accurate disclosure to your End Users of the privacy practices and policies applicable to the Application that is compliant with applicable law and these Developer Terms."

Guidelines (https://developers.tiktok.com/doc/our-guidelines-developer-guidelines): "Understand that the user's data belongs to them. You must safeguard their data. Don't share it with anyone without their proper consent." Never share PII without explicit user consent. "Protect the user's identity and anonymity." Never remove creator copyright mechanisms (e.g. watermarks).

Retention: "Personal Data will not be kept for longer than necessary." On termination, "delete TikTok Confidential Information or TikTok Information obtained through TikTok Developer Services in all forms in your possession and control (including from our servers)." No fixed day-count published for the Marketing API path (unlike Shopify's 30/48h). **VERIFY** the Business Products (Data) Terms for a concrete number.

You must also "actively maintain communication with TikTok when requested. Failure to respond to correspondence in a timely manner can lead to termination of your integration," and immediately acknowledge security/privacy/compliance correspondence. → a monitored, non-personal contact address must be the one on file.

### Brand — the tightest endorsement rule of the four
- Logo requires **prior written permission**. Third parties "may not use TikTok logos, icons, symbols, or designs without prior written permission."
- **"Never misguide users into thinking that you are part of the TikTok app."**
- Developer ToS: must not "imply any inaccurate affiliation, sponsorship, or endorsement of you or the Application by TikTok" **and cannot make public statements about their relationship with TikTok "without TikTok's prior written consent."**

That last clause is stronger than Shopify's or Woo's. Read literally, a public webpage saying "iGrowFast is a TikTok Marketing API partner" is a public statement about your relationship with TikTok and needs prior written consent. A purely functional, non-relational statement — "Connect your TikTok ad account" / "TikTok Ads integration" — is describing a feature, not asserting a relationship, and is the safe formulation. Use feature language, never relationship language.

### COD / dropshipping / lead-gen — the honest answer
**I found no official TikTok policy that prohibits or restricts COD, dropshipping, or lead-gen as advertiser business models.** The advertising policy index (https://ads.tiktok.com/help/article/tiktok-advertising-policies) enumerates 19 categories — Ad Format, Adult Content, Alcohol, Animals/Environment, Dangerous Products, Deceptive practices, Discrimination, Financial Services, Gambling, Healthcare, IP Infringement, Misinformation, Misleading and false content, Other Products and Services, Politics, Suicide/Self-Harm, Teen Safety, Violence, Weight Management — none of which is a COD/dropshipping/lead-gen category.

What *does* apply, from the After Conversion Experience Guidelines (https://ads.tiktok.com/help/article/commerce-policies):
- "Ensure that your pictures, videos, and all ad content accurately represent what you're offering"
- "Provide door-to-door shipping times, consider processing times, item availability, and shipping costs"
- "Clearly state return policies as advertised on your website"
- "Clearly communicate any potential expenses related to app features or services upfront"
- "If you source goods from suppliers, maintain quality control and ship on time as promised" ← the only dropshipping-adjacent line; it *contemplates* the model rather than banning it.

TikTok **Shop** COD is a different thing and is genuinely restricted (https://seller-ph.tiktok.com/university/essay?knowledge_id=7654197957265153): available only in select markets, **local-to-local transactions only**, and ineligible for large electronics, large furniture/appliances, perishables, intangibles (virtual products, services, warranties), and any product above a value threshold. **Morocco is not a TikTok Shop market** — so a TikTok Shop integration is not meaningfully available to your actual current user base. Marketing API (ads) is the realistic TikTok surface; TikTok Shop is aspirational at best. Don't put "TikTok Shop" on the website as a live integration.

Net: nothing prohibits your website from saying you serve COD sellers. What you cannot do is make earnings/guarantee claims — that's "Misleading and false content."

## SNAPCHAT

### Gate
Access is open — "Snap has made its Marketing API available to any developer (agency, brand, technology vendors, or individual)… now open to everyone," with "no longer restrictions on the minimum size and scope of what a developer must build" (https://businesshelp.snapchat.com/s/article/api-apply). Requires a **Business Account (Organization)** + an **OAuth app**.

But Snap Developer Terms (https://www.snap.com/terms/developer) retain a discretionary approval gate:
> "From time to time, Snap may require you to submit your Application for review and approval… Snap is under no obligation to approve your Application… Snap may reject, cease, or limit distribution of your Application at any time in its sole discretion without any liability to you."

And Business Tools Terms add prior-approval over the UI itself: partners must "obtain Snap's prior written approval of all aspects of the Application, including the user interface and the metrics displayed to customers prior to the Application being made available to Customers."

### The single most concrete privacy-policy requirement across all four platforms
Snap Developer Terms, verbatim:

> "You will provide and adhere to a published privacy policy for your Application that is easily accessible and conspicuously linked from the Application, **incorporates by reference and links to the Snap Privacy Policy**, and clearly and accurately describes to users of your Application what user information you and your Application access, collect, and store, and how and why you and your Application use, process, and share that information with Snap and other third parties."

Four distinct obligations land on your privacy policy page: (1) published + easily accessible; (2) conspicuously linked **from the app**, not just the marketing site — so an in-product footer/settings link, not only `igrowfast.com/privacy`; (3) **an explicit incorporation-by-reference clause plus a live hyperlink to https://www.snap.com/en-US/privacy/privacy-policy/**; (4) accurate description of what's accessed/collected/stored and how/why it's shared with Snap and third parties.

And from Snap Kit app review (https://developers.snap.com/snap-kit/app-review/submission-and-review): "Include a link to your app's Privacy Policy. **Links to another company's Privacy Policy or Snap Inc.'s Privacy Policy will not be accepted.**" — i.e. you need your own, AND it must link to Snap's. Both, not either.

### Data retention — hard numbers
- Business Services Data: "retain … for only as long as you have a legitimate business need" with a cap of "**thirty-six months**, or as otherwise provided in the documentation."
- "You will promptly delete all Snap Confidential Information and Business Services Data that is in your possession or control (including in your servers) upon request by Snap or upon termination of these Snap Developer Terms. **Upon Snap's request, you will certify your deletion and destruction.**" ← a certification capability, not just a delete button.
- Snap-side, for context (drives what you can promise): matched Pixel/CAPI data stored up to 13 months; unmatched deleted within 30 days; unmatched Customer List Audience data deleted after 30 days.
- Snap Kit: applications inactive >90 days are disconnected; users must re-authenticate.

### Customer contract flow-down
Partners must "have entered into a legally binding agreement with each Customer" that requires compliance with applicable law and Snap's terms. → **Your own ToS must contain a flow-down clause binding seller-clients to Snap's terms when they connect a Snap ad account.** Same pattern will be needed for TikTok. This is a Terms-of-Service structural requirement, not a privacy one.

Also: Business Services Data may only be used "for your benefit or the benefit of any party other than the Customer to whom the Business Services Data relates" when providing that customer access to services; aggregate modelling permitted only for that specific customer. → **no cross-tenant aggregation of Snap ad data.** Your existing per-business RLS isolation model already matches this; don't build a cross-business Snap benchmark feature.

### Brand
- "imply creation, affiliation, sponsorship, or endorsement of you or your Application by Snap or its affiliates" — prohibited.
- "make any statement or use the Snap Developer Program or any Snap Brand Features in any advertising or advertising product or to imply sponsorship by, endorsement from, or a false association with Snap" — prohibited.
- App review guidance: avoid incorporating "Snap's trademarks or brand indicia into your integration or integration title, **except for informational references**." → "Snapchat Ads integration" as a factual feature label is the permitted shape; "Snapchat Partner" is not.
- Only the official Ghost logo, from Snap's vault. **VERIFY** the PDF at https://www.snap.com/en-US/brand-guidelines before putting any Snap logo on the site. Default to text-only.
- On termination: "remove all Snap Brand Features from their application, and delete all metadata."
- Prohibited generally: sharing credentials outside your organization, exceeding reasonable request volumes, scraping, competing with Snap products, and generating "impressions, queries, clickthroughs, conversions… through any automated, deceptive, fraudulent, artificial, or otherwise invalid means."

## THE GENERIC-PROCESSOR-CATEGORY QUESTION — verdict per regime

Your constraint: disclose the EU-hosted messaging infrastructure provider only as a category, never by name. Verdict: **the constraint holds under all four platform regimes and under GDPR transparency law. It does NOT hold under your Article 28 processor obligations to your seller-clients — but that lands in the DPA, not on the website.**

Reasoning:

- **GDPR Art. 13(1)(e)/14(1)(e)** require disclosure of "the recipients **or categories of recipients**" of personal data. Categories are expressly permitted by the text. "Messaging infrastructure providers (EU-hosted)" is a lawful category disclosure for your *controller*-facing privacy notice. This is the load-bearing authority and it is squarely on your side.
- **Shopify**: only *recommends* disclosing "geographic location and data processing/storage locations" — a location, not a vendor identity. Protected-customer-data Level 1 requires you to "inform merchants what personal data you process and your reason for processing it" — again the *what/why*, not the *who*. **Category sufficient.**
- **WooCommerce**: §1.1.8 defers to "applicable law" and your own privacy policy; the marketplace privacy doc asks only that you disclose that extensions share data with third-party services (it names *categories*: "payment processors," "shipping providers," "third-party services"). **Category sufficient — and Woo's own doc models the category style.**
- **TikTok**: "complete and accurate disclosure … compliant with applicable law." Applicable law = GDPR = categories permitted. **Category sufficient.**
- **Snap**: "share that information **with Snap and other third parties**" — Snap's own drafting uses a generic bucket for everyone who isn't Snap. **Category sufficient for the messaging provider.**

The asymmetry, and it's the sharpest point here: **the platforms themselves cannot be generic categories.** Snap contractually requires you to *name Snap and hyperlink Snap's privacy policy* and incorporate it by reference. Shopify, TikTok, Meta and the AI vendors should likewise be named — a reviewer reading "we share data with advertising platforms" while your app clearly posts to their API will read that as evasive and it invites exactly the scrutiny you're avoiding. So: **name every platform you integrate; keep the messaging vendor as a category.** That's a coherent, defensible, non-arbitrary line — platform integrations are user-visible and user-initiated; the messaging transport is an implementation detail.

Where the category *fails*: **Art. 28(2)** — a processor "shall not engage another processor without prior specific or general written authorisation of the controller," and under general authorisation must "inform the controller of any intended changes concerning the addition or replacement of other processors, thereby giving the controller the opportunity to object." Your seller-clients are controllers of their customers' data; you are their processor; the messaging vendor is your **sub-processor**. To give a controller a real right to object, they must know who they'd be objecting to. In practice this is satisfied by a **named sub-processor list furnished to clients under the DPA** — which can be a gated/authenticated page, an annex to the DPA, or "available on request," none of which is your public marketing site. Shopify Protected-Customer-Data Level 1 independently forces this: "Make privacy and data protection agreements with your merchants."

So the operational answer: public privacy page = category. DPA annex to seller-clients = named. These are different documents with different audiences and there is no contradiction.

## JURISDICTION REALITY CHECK

Two mismatches that will surface, and neither is a platform rule — they're what a reviewer/regulator notices:

1. **The Wyoming shell vs. the actual operation.** 30 N Gould St Ste R, Sheridan WY 82801 is one of the most heavily-used mass registered-agent addresses in the US; thousands of entities share it. TikTok (business registration documents for higher-volume access), Snap (Business Account/Organization) and Shopify all run business verification. A WY LLC at a known agent address, with no US staff, servers in Germany, and a Moroccan user base, is a profile that gets extra scrutiny. Nothing here is prohibited — but do not build the website's credibility on the US-company framing alone. Have the German hosting and the actual operating footprint stated plainly; the mismatch is only damaging when it looks concealed.

2. **GDPR applies regardless of the Wyoming incorporation.** Servers in Germany = establishment in the Union (Art. 3(1)) — processing "in the context of the activities of an establishment" — and even setting that aside, Art. 3(2) catches monitoring/offering. The US-LLC wrapper buys nothing here. Consequences that land on the website: a privacy policy that actually satisfies Art. 13, an **Art. 27 EU representative** question (Art. 3(1) establishment via the German servers likely means you don't need one — but that hinges on whether the Contabo VPSs constitute an "establishment," which is a legal call, not mine to make), and the EU→wherever transfer story. Get counsel on the Art. 27 point specifically; it's the kind of thing that's cheap to fix now and embarrassing later.

3. **WhatsApp message content is the highest-risk data class you hold** — it's end-customer *communications content*, not just contact data. Your blind-HMAC keyword search index (migs 067a/067b) is a good design precisely because it keeps plaintext out of backups; say so on the privacy page in plain language ("message search operates on irreversible keyed hashes; message content is not stored in our search index"). That's a genuine differentiator and it directly answers the question every reviewer will ask.
